Holiday baking can go beyond cookies
articles.description: Baked goods and the holiday season go hand in hand. Many families incorporate baking into their holiday traditions. There’s no limit to the treats that can be baked come the […]
articles.content: Baked goods and the holiday season go hand in hand. Many families incorporate baking into their holiday traditions. There’s no limit to the treats that can be baked come the holiday season, but families who want to offer something less traditional can try this recipe for pecan brownies with icing sugar from Lines+Angles. Pecan brownies with icing sugarFrom Metro Creative Connection Pecan brownies with icing sugar 12 ounces plain dark chocolate, 70% cocoa solids 9 ounces butter Three large eggs 9 ounces dark brown sugar 2 ounces flour 1 teaspoon baking powder 5 ounces chopped pecans To decorate: Icing sugar 1. Heat the oven to 325 degrees. Grease a 7-by-11-inch baking dish and line the base with non-stick baking paper. 2. Put the chocolate and butter in a pan and heat gently, stirring until melted. Allow to cool slightly. 3. Whisk the eggs in a mixing bowl until pale and frothy, then add the sugar a spoonful at a time, whisking until thick and glossy. 4. Gently fold in the melted chocolate mixture. Sift in the flour and baking powder and fold in the pecans. 5. Spoon the mixture into the baking dish, level with the back of a spoon and bake for 40 minutes, until the top has a cracked appearance and the center is still a little soft to the touch. Do not overbake, or you will lose the famous sticky brownie texture. Cool in the pan. 6. Cut into slices and sift over a little icing sugar.

articles.title: Assembly adds to the charm of downtown Mason
articles.description: By GABRIELLE LAWRENCE A girlfriend of mine recently asked me what the main storyline would be if I wrote the story of my life. I told her one of the […]
articles.content: By GABRIELLE LAWRENCE A girlfriend of mine recently asked me what the main storyline would be if I wrote the story of my life. I told her one of the themes would be that I chose to stay in my hometown. Many people who I have known since childhood have moved away, some to different areas of Michigan but many to different states. Although I lived overseas in my 20s and briefly bounced around Southeast Michigan, Mr. She Ate and I have made Lansing our home. That very conscious choice has affected so many parts of my life, from how I spend my non-working hours to the opportunities that I will pursue for my own children to how I talk about my city to other people. This column is a natural extension of that. Mason’s Assembly is quickly becoming known for its fish and chips, which both She Ate/He Ate reviewers thoroughly enjoyed. Bryan Beverly for City Pulse Pre-pandemic, my reviews were sometimes much more harsh than what is now printed. I didn’t ever relish bashing a local restaurant, but now I pay a lot more attention to the power that my words have. That’s not to suggest that I don’t offer criticism when it is warranted, but as an example of how this column has evolved, a few weeks ago B (known to many of you as “He Ate”) and I pulled the plug on reviewing a newish spot because my experience there was so awful. I don’t feel the need to pile on, and I will instead work doubly hard to promote other places that are earning it. Since becoming a county commissioner four years ago, I’ve driven to downtown Mason a few times a month for board of commissioners meetings. Frequently, I will grab a slice of pizza, a sandwich or a salad at Westside Deli, which is both nostalgic for me and also reliably delicious. However, I’ve been dreaming about a very niche place I want to see in Mason. It’s just about the most picturesque, cozy town on Earth, and I want to sit and dig into a hearty lunch or dinner on a snowy day, watching the shoppers rush home with their treasures. And readers, Assembly is here to do this for us. Mr. She Ate and I got an early-bird Saturday-night babysitter in the form of my trusty and generous dad and headed to Assembly for dinner. We were surprised but charmed by the intimacy of the small restaurant and immediately got good vibes from our server, who was attentive and intuitive but not overbearing. We started with blistered Brussels sprouts ($12) and whipped ricotta ($12) appetizers. The Brussels were pleasantly salty and topped with pickled shallot, which is a combination I had never considered but one that worked perfectly. The whipped ricotta was spread thick on a slice of toasted sourdough, then sprinkled with lemon zest, chili oil and chopped pistachios. The flavors were spot on. I particularly appreciated that the toast was sliced into fingers, which made inhaling the dish much easier. Mr. She Ate and I decided to order the fish and chips ($19) and steak frites ($35) to share. The portion of fish was huge, and we took a good half of it home, to be inadvertently stuck in the back of our fridge and never heard from again. Isn’t that just the way of things sometimes? The batter was slightly sweet, which I liked. The steak was perfectly (and I mean perfectly) cooked to my requested medium rare. I did have to dig into my ever-present supply of sea salt that I keep in a tin in my purse in order to add a bit more to the dish, but that was more due to personal preference. Assembly – Hours and contact 402 S. Jefferson St., Mason 11 a.m.-9 p.m. Monday-Thursday 11 a.m.-11 p.m. Friday-Saturday 10 a.m.-9 p.m. Sunday (517) 604-6070 assemblymason.com We didn’t love the fries. They weren’t well seasoned, and the presentation could use some retooling. They were served underneath the steak in a pool of jus, which left them soggy and unappetizing. I would prefer them to be served in the French bistro style, shockingly crispy and piled high next to the steak. I chose our dessert methodically, eschewing the delicious Mr. Leslie’s Cheesecake for something housemade in order to test Assembly’s chops further. I already know that I love Mr. Leslie’s extraordinary cheesecakes, so we asked for the crème brûlée ($10). To be fair, I’m not generally dazzled by crème brûlée. It’s vanilla custard. I’m all for a classic, but give me something with some character. However, Assembly’s version had a depth of lusciousness that I wasn’t expecting, and I have no notes other than “would order again.” In ancillary but crowd-pleasing news, Mr. She Ate was pleasantly surprised by the reasonable drink prices. His chosen beer was $5, and because of that, he had two of them. We were home by 7:30, glowing in the aftermath of a wonderful experience at a new local restaurant, and were able to put the kids to bed on time. She Ate / He Ate – City Pulse By BRYAN BEVERLY Mason seems to have more than its share of culinary destinations, and every now and then, a new restaurant comes along that gives you yet another reason to make the trip downtown. Such is the case with Assembly, the latest venture from Greater Lansing restaurateur Matt Gillett. A little bit gastropub and a little bit neighborhood gathering place, it’s a welcome addition to a small town with a growing culinary identity. Assembly has a new American aesthetic that strikes a nice balance between old-school character and contemporary style. Exposed brick provides a sense of history and warmth, while modern fixtures, thoughtfully selected finishes and distinctive lighting give the space a more polished, metropolitan feel. It’s comfortable without being overly casual and stylish without trying too hard. The location is another part of the appeal. A short distance from the Ingham County Courthouse and government complex, Assembly has the potential to become a regular stop for courthouse visitors, county employees, local professionals and residents alike. And then there’s Gillett, who’s never been content to simply repeat a successful formula. With Saddleback BBQ, Slice by Saddleback and Coach’s Pub & Grill, he has demonstrated a willingness to explore different concepts and give each one its own identity. What makes Gillett’s continued expansion particularly noteworthy is that his involvement in the community extends beyond opening restaurant doors. He recognizes that local business owners play a role in creating spaces where people gather, connect and invest in the places they call home. His decision to bring Assembly to Mason feels consistent with that philosophy. It’s an investment in a downtown that deserves attention and a restaurant that can contribute to the city’s continued momentum. What’s decent A colleague and I stopped into Assembly on a brisk afternoon for a late lunch. George, our server, was friendly and eager to discuss the menu. He recommended some starters, and we settled on the confit garlic arancini ($11), the pork belly ($13) and the whipped ricotta ($12) before catching up on professional and personal matters. The arancini is not for the weak of palate (or those who don’t carry mints). The deep-fried risotto balls were stuffed with parmesan cheese and plenty of garlic. My first bite, while satisfyingly crispy on the outside and silky on the inside, almost took my breath away with its bitter pungency, and the accompanying aioli was a creamy excess of garlic. The whipped ricotta was equally up and down, with the creamy cheese providing a velvety, sweet indulgence and the pistachios and chili oil providing a balance of textures and flavors. However, the “toasted” sourdough was anything but as it wilted underneath. What’s better The mushroom risotto ($22) presented well. Both the plating and the cook of the grains were spot on. The cremini and shitake mushrooms were just firm enough, and the fried onion crisps offered a nice crunch. Yet it took multiple dashes of table salt to provide any flavor. The dish was a bit flat without it. The fish and chips ($19) were much better. Two massive pollock fillets crisscrossed over a bed of hand-cut french fries. The housemade tartar sauce was delightful, and the fish was tender and flaky, with a perfectly crunchy exterior. Best bite Earlier, I mentioned the pork belly starter, which is a winning dish. Chunks of pork belly slathered in a sweet barbecue sauce and dusted with chopped pistachios sat atop a puree of root vegetables mixed with stone fruit. This combination of sweet, smoky and bright is what pushing the envelope is all about.

Willie Johnson finds catharsis in revisiting past traumas
articles.description: Military veteran Willie Johnson didn’t want his children to guess who he was or why he was the way he was. That’s one of the reasons he wrote “I Was […]
articles.content: Military veteran Willie Johnson didn’t want his children to guess who he was or why he was the way he was. That’s one of the reasons he wrote “I Was There: Echoes of a Broken Boy.” Johnson published the memoir through LivOutUrDream LLC, a creative brand he founded in late 2025 dedicated to storytelling, music and personal transformation. Willie Johnson. Courtesy “Writing gives them something they can come back to. It gives our family a record beyond the things we happened to talk about,” Johnson said. “And for somebody outside my family, I hope the book says this: You can be carrying a lot and still have something to give. I was there. I am here. And I’m still working on what comes next.” The impetus to write “I Was There” came while attending grief counseling after the death of his father. However, he explained that there was so much more connected to it. He felt like he needed to go back to the beginning. “I started putting down what I remembered,” he said. “I used conversations with ChatGPT to help unpack the memories and organize them into chapters, and I asked family members questions as things came back to me. I also wanted to look back and ask where God had been through all of it. What started as trying to understand my own life became ‘I Was There.’” More about Willie Johnson Born and raised in Washington, D.C., Willie Johnson is the second of four children. He lives in Lansing with his wife of nine years. The couple has five children, ages 20, 19, 16, 8 and 7. Johnson is a graduate of Dunbar High School, where he participated in JROTC and the armed drill team. He completed some coursework at Prince George’s Community College in Largo, Maryland. From 2005 to 2009, he served in the D.C. National Guard. He started as a motor transport operator and later worked as an automated logistical specialist. His service included Hurricane Katrina relief and deployment to Iraq. His final rank was specialist (E-4), and his discharge from the military was general under honorable conditions. “JROTC gave me structure and a sense of belonging,” he said. “When I joined the D.C. National Guard, I saw a way to serve my country, learn a practical skill and still help my family. My grandmother depended on me, so those responsibilities were part of the decision.” A Washington, D.C., native, Johnson grew up around addiction, incarceration, violence and loss. “My mother was shot while she was pregnant with me, so the story begins before I could even remember it,” he said. “Later, I lost her while I was still a child. My father was incarcerated during parts of my childhood, and my grandparents stepped in to raise us. There was love in that home, but there was also grief I didn’t know how to handle. I dealt with bullying and fighting, and I learned to put a hard face on things. As a boy, I didn’t have the words to explain what I was carrying. A lot of that pain came out as anger.” Admittedly, he is still working through a lot. “I can get up, take care of people and look like I have everything together while there is still a lot happening inside. That’s something I’ve had to be honest about,” he said. “My faith, my wife and children, counseling and writing have all been part of that work. The military taught me discipline, but I also had to learn that being able to keep going doesn’t mean I’ve dealt with everything. Asking for help and looking at those memories gave me a way to start understanding them.” “I Was There: Echoes of a Broken Boy” by Willie Johnson Writing “I Was There” was cathartic. At the same time, it was also difficult. “Writing brought back things I hadn’t thought about in years and some things I didn’t remember until I started talking. There were moments when I had to stop,” Johnson explained. “Writing about my brother’s death was one of the hardest parts. I got to that chapter and struggled to move forward. There’s a difference between knowing something happened and sitting down long enough to put it into words. “I also had to think about the people who are still here,” he continued. “This is my experience, but other people lived parts of it with me. I wanted to be honest without being careless with them.” He was especially worried about hurting his beloved grandmother. “But she read the finished book — I think she read it four times — and our relationship grew stronger. That meant a lot to me,” he said. Writing the memoir helped him connect parts of his life that he’d been carrying separately. “I could see how that little boy’s grief followed me into being a soldier, a husband and a father,” he said. “It follows the connections between childhood in D.C., military service, family, grief and faith. You see the boy before you see the soldier, and you see how what happened to him affected the man he became. I wanted to be honest about the parts that are hard to say out loud. I’m still learning, and that’s in the story, too. Putting it into words didn’t erase what happened, but it helped me understand myself. I hope someone reading it can recognize something of themselves and feel that their own story matters.” He spoke about founding LivOutUrDream. “A friend of mine used the phrase ‘live out your dream loud,’ and it stayed with me. I know what it feels like to have ideas and experiences inside you without knowing how to bring them out. Learning to publish my own story showed me that I could help someone else do it, too,” he said. “LOUD brings together storytelling, publishing, music and family creativity. I’ve helped with my son’s comic and a fellow veteran’s cookbook. I want people to see that their stories and their ideas are worth doing something with. For me, that’s part of building a legacy.” Johnson is working on his second memoir, “I Am Here,” which chronicles his family’s move to Michigan. He is also adapting “I Was There” into a graphic novel. In the long run, he wants to turn the memoir interview process into a workbook or a class that helps people explore their lives and preserve their family histories. “Through LOUD, I want to keep helping other people bring their work into the world,” he said. He gave some advice to people who have endured great trauma and hardship and want to write about it. “Start with what you can say. You don’t have to explain your whole life at once,” he said. “Talk to someone you trust, ask for help, or write something down if that’s where you can begin. I know what it is to put the face back on and go take care of the next person. But you need care, too. Give yourself room to get it. Your story matters — even the parts you haven’t figured out how to tell yet.”

articles.title: Escape from New York: Joshua Gersen brings metropolitan mojo to Lansing Symphony
articles.description: In February 2017, Joshua Gersen made an unexpected and dramatic subscription concert debut with the New York Philharmonic. In the middle of a time-crunched rehearsal that was pushed to late […]
articles.content: In February 2017, Joshua Gersen made an unexpected and dramatic subscription concert debut with the New York Philharmonic. In the middle of a time-crunched rehearsal that was pushed to late afternoon by a snowstorm, music director Semyon Bychkov fell ill and was taken to the hospital. Gersen finished the rehearsal and mounted the podium a couple of hours later to conduct Tchaikovsky’s epic “Pathétique” symphony, which he’d never conducted before, and two other works. When it was all over, the orchestra stood and applauded his last-minute heroics. The New York Times called the performance “passionate and incisive.” Former New York Philharmonic assistant conductor Joshua Gersen is the third of five guest conductors leading the Lansing Symphony Orchestra this season to determine who will fill the shoes of departing music director Timothy Muffitt. Photo by Chris Lee Gersen faces a slightly less nerve-wracking challenge Saturday, as the third of five guest conductors leading the Lansing Symphony Orchestra this season to determine who will fill the shoes of departing music director Timothy Muffitt. “Working together for the first time is a bit like a first date,” Gersen said. “Sometimes you lock in, and sometimes it takes a bit of time to get on the same page. It’s the unknown. All you can do is go in there and do your thing, do what you do the best you can.” Gersen’s tenure as assistant conductor in New York ended in 2018. He has enjoyed being the music director of the New York Youth Symphony, taking the group on its first international tour in 50 seasons, and guest conducting with the San Francisco Symphony, the Chicago Symphony and many other ensembles, but he’s ready for new horizons. “I’m from (New York), and I’ve been here for quite a while, but I’m looking for the next chapter, hoping to find an orchestra to work with regularly,” Gersen said. He has worked several times with the Detroit Symphony, including a 2019 screening of “Jaws” with John Williams’ famous score performed live, and done conducting workshops in Ann Arbor, but he’s never been to Lansing. “Talking to the administration and the committee in Lansing, I was really impressed with how organized, how stable everything seems to be there,” he said. “They’re in good shape in many ways and looking to grow the ensemble, and that’s exactly the kind of situation I’m looking for.” In the wider world, conducting is a rare life choice, but for Gersen, it was inevitable. He started conducting — and reading scores — when he was 3 years old. An early hero was the charismatic New York Philharmonic maestro Leonard Bernstein. “For me and my family, a Jewish family in New York City, he was incredibly important, our champion in many ways,” Gersen said. “At the centennial of his birthday, I actually got to conduct ‘West Side Story’ with the New York Philharmonic, and that was really special for me.” Another early influence was Gustav Meier, music director of the Lansing Symphony from 1978 to 2006. “I was very, very lucky that he happened to be conducting the Bridgeport Symphony in Connecticut when I was growing up right around there,” Gersen said. “I got in touch with him and got to study with him all through high school, and he was a really important person in my life growing up.” On the podium, Gersen is muscular, grounded and precise. “There are a lot of conductors out there who are a little more flamboyant in their gestures than I tend to be,” he said. “But for me, it’s about studying the music and, when I’m up there, trying to recreate the music as the composer wanted to hear it and helping the musicians on stage play the best they can. It’s not about me at all.” Gersen is impressed by the innovative programs the Lansing Symphony established during Muffitt’s tenure, such as the composer-in-residence program and the new music series LSO at The Robin. He hopes to extend the orchestra’s reach further with concerts and casual events in non-traditional venues around the community. “The biggest problem we run into, as far as attracting a broader audience, is that many people still feel like it’s some kind of elitist club they don’t belong to,” he said. “Anything we can do to make everybody feel welcome, make it an enjoyable experience, is important.” He’s happy to talk from the stage about the music on the program, and he likes the idea of turning pre-concert talks into podcasts people can listen to in the car on the way to the concert hall. “There are so many interesting things about the music we’re performing,” he said, and he’d like to make people aware of that “any way we can.” For Saturday’s concert, Gersen picked three works that, in his view, “deliver a universal message.” Chris Rogerson wrote the evening’s opener, “Noble Pond,” after the tragic death in 2007 of 5-year-old Austin Haley, who was fishing with his grandfather in an Oklahoma pond when a police officer fired at a snake nearby and a bullet struck him. The simple lyricism and beauty of “Noble Pond” often reduces audiences to a reverent silence. “Chris is a very good friend of mine. We went to school together,” Gersen said. “He’s a wonderful composer whose music should be played more often.” Gersen said the other works on the program, Sibelius’ violin concerto and Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony, “are obviously kind of iconic and don’t need much introduction” but build on the same emotional arc. “It’s a program about overcoming adversity,” Gersen said. “Chris’ piece is about a specific tragic event. Sibelius’ concerto was written when he was going through a lot of things personally, and he was wistfully lamenting the fact that he could never play violin himself. And, of course, the Beethoven Fifth is the quintessential example of humans facing the greatest adversity and triumphing over it. It’s a very heavy but uplifting program.”

articles.title: It’s gotta be the shoes: All of the Above Hip Hop Academy’s Sneaker Gala showcases its future
articles.description: It can be nice to get all dressed up with somewhere to go in Lansing. And nicer still if that somewhere is a fun, one-of-a-kind event that brings positivity to […]
articles.content: It can be nice to get all dressed up with somewhere to go in Lansing. And nicer still if that somewhere is a fun, one-of-a-kind event that brings positivity to our youth. All of the Above Hip Hop Academy held its fourth annual Sneaker Gala fundraiser at Lansing Shuffle in late October. About 250 attendees paired their classiest formal wear with their coolest designer sneakers to help the nonprofit raise donations to support its free youth programming. Seen at the gala: Jose Aste, owner of Tantay Peruvian Cuisine; Ozay Moore, executive director of All of the Above Hip Hop Academy; and Christina Castilla, AOTA teaching artist. Photo by Mr. Joe Walker for City Pulse All of the Above, among other things, connects young people with mentors who help to expand their universe of potential. Its programs provide a supplemental arts education led by established working artists and educators, with offerings including dance, music production and more. AOTA executive director Ozay Moore said the organization holds the annual gala to tell the stories, not just to raise money. “We know the resources and the support come not just in one night, but throughout the year,” Moore said. “That’s why we love doing it, and that’s why we love our community, because they show up for us beyond just one night.” At the gala, the foundational elements of hip-hop culture — emceeing, deejaying, breaking, graffiti arts, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, love, peace, unity and having fun — were on full display. All of the Above Hip Hop Academy instructors NewSense (Leah Koski), left, and Alien J (Janeil Foy) strike a pose at the organization’s Sneaker Gala. Photo by Mr. Joe Walker for City Pulse “The night was a celebration of our community, the work we do, the vision, the mission and the people who are on the inside making it happen,” Moore said. “A celebration of the community partners who, quite literally, give us space to demonstrate what we believe, and that’s that hip-hop has transformational powers. It has the ability to shape our community, shape our young people, shape our minds and really bring folks together.” Backed by a list of sponsors that included LAFCU, PNC Bank, TechSmith, Sigma Financial Corp., Bellwether Public Relations, the Indigenous Youth Empowerment Program, Downtown Lansing Inc. and E&S, the gala saw AOTA students take center stage to showcase what they’ve learned for a receptive audience. In turn, the audience showered the students with an impressive ovation. All of the Above Youth Organization teaching artist Alexis Rosado served as the gala’s emcee. With the best seat in the house, Rosado said she got to see up close the bravery, confidence and boldness of the students. “I feel like the students stole the show,” Rosado said. “It was so cool to see smiling faces looking back at the students showcasing their joy. It was all about the students. I also got to see good fits, good vibes and cool sneakers.” Arguably the coolest shoes of the night were showcased during the sneaker auction. A custom pair is donated each year by Detroit b-boy Sneaker Tek. This year, he contributed vivid Nike Cortez shoes emblazoned with the elements of hip-hop. They were claimed for $1,500. AOTA programs and operations manager Carla Brooks said it’s easy to see the future of the organization’s programming because she’s already witnessed it. “At the first gala, I was just blown away and excited by what I was seeing, and now I’m seeing students that are now teachers,” Brooks said. “At the same time, I don’t know where else we’re going. But, as hip-hop says, ‘Hip-hop goes where the people go.’ I don’t know what’s next, but I’m here for it.” Visit alloftheabovehiphop.org to donate and for programming info.

articles.title: Bruce Springsteen fan club disbands after ‘The Boss’ endorses Abdul El-Sayed
articles.content: A sizable Bruce Springsteen fan club that’s been active for more than a decade is calling it quits because of the “Born in the USA” singer’s politics. The Spring-Nuts’ organizers blame The Boss’s support for Michigan Senator-elect Abdul Al-Sayed for pushing them too far. “As Bruce became more outspoken about his politics, something we understood and respected as his absolute right, we found ourselves facing a difficult balancing act,” fan club founder Howie Chaz told the Asbury Park Press. Chaz, who ran the organization with his wife Julia, reportedly accused Springsteen of engaging in rhetoric that caused division among the nearly 20,000 Facebook followers on their feed who initially bonded over The Boss’s words and music. The group’s social media page was inactive on Monday. Chaz told the Bruce Springsteen Center for American Music in September that he met his wife through the fan club he launched in 2011. “Today, across all of our social media platforms, the Spring-Nuts community has grown to more than 70,000 people worldwide,” he told that organization. The Spring-Nuts reportedly got a shoutout from The Boss via video during a fundraiser at Asbury Park’s famed Stone Pony music club in 2022. Springsteen’s E-Street Band guitarist “Little” Steven Van Zandt appeared with the Chens on their “Spring-Nut Cafe” podcast in August. He thanked its members for their support. “You know, it’s a mutual … energy exchange, man,” Van Zandt said. “Without your guys enthusiasm, you know, what are we doing, right? So, you guys matter just as much… for your enthusiasm and your supporting us. So I can speak on behalf of the E Street Band and everybody else I’m involved with.” Springsteen endorsed Al-Sayed earlier this month. “Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution, he’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House,” the rock star posted on Instagram. “That’s why I’m in his corner 100%.” El-Sayed critics largely express concerns about the Democratic leader’s opposition to Israel’s actions in Gaza. President Trump — who has a famously strained relationship with Springsteen — has accused El-Sayed of being “on the side of the terrorists.” Springsteen’s representatives haven’t responded to a request for comment.

articles.title: Michigan economic group won't renew Israel business accelerator contract, citing tight budget
articles.description: Critics of the Michigan Economic Development Corporation's grant to the Michigan Israel Business Accelerator accused the group of working with companies that benefit Israel’s military operations.
articles.content: The Michigan Israel Business Accelerator hosts a delegation of Israeli municipal leaders in Detroit as part of an international exchange program in August 2026.( Michigan Israel Business Accelerator)A state-supported grant for attracting Israeli business investment will not be moving forward next year. The announcement came Tuesday during a monthly Michigan Economic Development Corporation executive committee meeting.Finance subcommittee chair Lizabeth Ardisana told the board that the budget had gotten tight and that the cuts did not single out any one organization.“There were a number of programs that were not funded, particularly business accelerators. That doesn’t mean that those programs can’t continue to look for funding in the future, possibly under a new administration,” Ardisana said.The Michigan Israel Business Accelerator’s current $650,000 MEDC grant will expire at the end of December. After that, the accelerator's CEO Mark Davidoff said the group plans to move forward while looking for other funding sources.“We have a full strategy and operational plan for 2027 and we’re going to execute that with full precision and we’re going to continue to be as competitive as we can be,” Davidoff said in an interview.While the MEDC’s funding decision affects multiple development organizations, MIBA had received significant scrutiny during public comment in recent meetings. Critics of its grant accused the group of working with companies that benefit Israel’s military operations, and called that country's human rights record into question.During public comment Tuesday, dozens of speakers urged the MEDC to not leave the door open for the Michigan Israel Business Accelerator to receive future funds.Commission members did not indicate that public comment weighed on the decision at all. Davidoff emphasized the business accelerator's work is about helping Michigan’s businesses and economy grow.“It has nothing to do with the foreign policy agenda of the United States and military support of the state of Israel of any nature. It’s about supporting the U.S. military and our soldiers in the field and our first responders,” Davidoff said.The group's website lists mobility, U.S. aerospace and national security, and advanced manufacturing as some of the top sectors where Israel and the U.S. can partner. Others include health technology, agriculture, and sustainability.Several of its own grants are available in each area. Some awards total more than $1 million.The terms of its active grant require it to boost the value of Michigan-Israel economic activity by at least 20% over 2025. The contract also calls for the onboarding of “at least 10 new Israeli companies.”When asked Tuesday how many new companies had partnered with Michigan this year, Davidoff didn’t have a number handy. He said over the past five years, the group brought over $45 million in economic development into Michigan through its partnerships.

Ken Griffin, target of Zohran Mamdani, has officially sold his $58 million apartment to NY Jets owner
articles.content: You gotta hand it to Zohran Mamdani. He may not be smart, competent or honest, but he is extremely capable of pushing people out of New York City. The current mayor of New York, who's spent his time in office purposefully looking for ways to make life in the city worse, made it one of his top priorities to try and punish wealthy residents who own second homes there. That punishment, short-sighted and nonsensical as it is, focused on taking money from those with properties in the city that aren't main residences with his so-called "pied-à-terre" tax. Mamdani's campaign of absurdity started earlier in 2026 by directly targeting one of the wealthiest people in the country, billionaire hedge fund manager Ken Griffin, CEO of Citadel. Griffin has created thousands of jobs in New York, contributing untold billions to the local economy. He also had plans to build a $6 billion office building in Manhattan to supplant his firm's new headquarters in Miami. Trump faces GOP pushback to his order to use steam to launch jets from aircraft carriers
articles.description: Trump faces GOP pushback to his order to use steam to launch jets from aircraft carriers AP News Reverting Ford-class Carriers to Steam is ‘Non-Starter,’ Says SASC Chair Wicker USNI News Lawmakers challenge Trump’s push to bring steam catapults back to Ford-class carriers Breaking Defense Key Republican Rejects Trump Order on Steam-Driven Launch System Bloomberg.com Trump's Demand For Steam Catapults On New Carriers
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Senators want to scuttle President Donald Trump’s order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults to launch fighter jets, a directive that would cost billions of taxpayer dollars and could even blunt the lethality of America’s most advanced warships. Sen. Roger Wicker, the Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, put it plainly at a hearing Tuesday: “Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that.” Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee also made clear their opposition to Trump’s steam catapult directive in the 2027 defense appropriations bill, which was released Monday. The bill would direct the Navy to provide a report on the effectiveness of the new, magnetically powered catapult system that shoots fighter jets off the deck of carriers versus the old steam-powered one. “The Committee is concerned that such a major redesign would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays,” Republican lawmakers wrote in an explanatory statement about Trump’s order. The pushback in the waning days of the Republican-controlled Congress is a notable rebuke to one of Trump’s pet issues. He claimed that the magnetic catapults “didn’t work” during remarks in the Oval Office last year, issued the memo in August directing a return to the old steam system and has a long history of railing against the technology. It comes as the Republican president tries to convince Congress to pass his $1.5 trillion defense budget before the end of the year. Democrats will take control of the House and Senate on Jan. 3, setting the stage for battles over spending in Washington. In a statement accompanying the defense spending bill, Republicans on the Appropriations Committee targeted Trump’s steam catapult order and warned against “such significant programmatic shifts without substantive analysis, justification, and Congressional approval.” The statement also noted what lawmakers and experts have been saying: The fighting in Iran appeared to show that the new electromagnetic system on the nation’s most advanced aircraft carrier, the USS Gerald R. Ford, launched more planes in less time and with fewer sailors than the steam catapults of older carriers. The new technology also appeared to demonstrate greater “combat lethality than previous generation carriers,” the GOP lawmakers said. The steam catapult issue came up Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering Trump’s nomination of acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to permanently take the top civilian job. Under questioning from Sen. Tim Kaine, a Democrat from Virginia, Cao appeared to stand behind Trump’s directive, arguing that including the new system, along with electromagnetically driven elevators, was “delaying our carriers by seven years.” “I’m trying to accelerate that,” he added. While the new systems experienced development delays during the USS Ford’s construction, Navy leaders have praised their performance and maintenance following the carrier’s recent deployment to the Middle East. Imposing changes to the Ford-class design appears to continue what the administration’s own assessment found to be one of the issues facing American shipbuilding. Trump’s August memo noted that the Navy’s constant design changes “have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.” “The Navy shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs,” the memo declared. When asked about the pushback to the directive, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said: “President Trump has revitalized America’s shipbuilding industry, which is essential to the national security and economic prosperity of the United States. President Trump has fixed critical long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding, and will continue to restore American maritime dominance.” Cao’s support for Trump’s order seemed in contrast to the acting Navy secretary’s arguments earlier in the hearing, when he touted his decision to halt all engineering changes to the Navy’s new frigates to keep that program on track. When asked about the contradicting testimony, Lt. Cmdr. Adagray Willis, a spokeswoman for Cao, said Cao would work with the White House, Pentagon, Congress and the defense industry “to ensure ours remains the fiercest Navy in the world.” At the hearing, Kaine spoke out against Trump’s steam directive and noted his conversations with sailors on the flight deck of the USS Ford who spoke “very highly” of the new system. Kaine represents the Ford’s homeport of Norfolk as well as the city headquartering the only company building U.S. aircraft carriers, Newport News Shipbuilding. “I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford before you decide to go down on a path that will be more expensive and less capable,” Kaine told Cao. Trump’s August directive to remove the electromagnetic system and return to steam raised concerns about costs as well as the difficulty of maintaining the older systems, which need more sailors to operate them. His ire with the new technology goes back to at least 2017 in his first term, when he claimed the new system is “not good” and “doesn’t have the power” of the older, steam systems. “You’re going to goddamned steam,” Trump said in an interview with Time magazine. The topic has frequently come up since then at rallies and other events. In April, Cao’s predecessor, Secretary John Phelan, announced the Navy was reviewing the design and costs of the Ford-class aircraft carrier and was not ruling out canceling future versions of its design. The newest Chinese aircraft carriers employ electromagnetic catapults, and France said it plans to use the system on its new carrier.

articles.title: Aidan Hutchinson's ACL tear sparks a celebration debate that Dan Campbell won't escalate
articles.description: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell says he won't ban celebrations after Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL celebrating a sack. Campbell, who once tore a biceps celebrating, believes freak injuries happen.
articles.content: Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) sits on the field after picking up an injury as he celebrated a sack on New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) during an NFL football game in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader)(Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/Matthias Schrader / AP)Freak injuries can occur anytime, anywhere.So, Lions coach Dan Campbell said Tuesday, he's not about to impose a celebration ban after star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson tore his right ACL celebrating a sack Sunday in Detroit's big win over New England in Munich.Campbell noted he once tore a biceps pumping his arm in celebration as a player."You’ve got to be smart about it, but sometimes, man, things happen," Campbell said after confirming Hutchinson's season is over. "How do we know it wasn’t going to be the next play? You see guys, they make some of the most explosive movements under pressure, under stress, being tied up with another person. For that one to be the one (where he gets hurt), it’s crazy.“So, no, I’m not going to make a big deal of this. It’s unfortunate. I hate it for Hutch," Campbell added. "But I don’t think we need to have some big PowerPoint and lesson about how to celebrate, how not to celebrate. Guys, let’s be smart. You know, understand what it is. Don’t put yourself in jeopardy. Let’s not do backflips. That would be one (to eliminate). Let’s not do that.”That's exactly the recommendation the New York Giants made to rising star running back Cam Skattebo, whose botched backflip in the offseason got him in hot water with coach John Harbaugh and general manger Joe Schoen.Skattebo was coming back from surgery to repair a broken fibula and a dislocated ankle when he landed awkwardly on his surgically repaired right ankle after doing his signature celebration at Fanatics Fest in New York just before reporting to training camp.He turned out to be fine, but the Giants were none too pleased with him.“The big picture message is you want to take care of yourself,” Harbaugh said. “You want to take care of your team. Do everything you can do to be healthy, be back, be right, be good.”Skattebo has resumed doing backflips and he said last week he now feels 100% healthy.Hutchinson's injury brought back memories of Bill Gramatica, who was kicking for the Arizona Cardinals in 2001 when he celebrated a 42-yard field goal by jumping into the air. He landed awkwardly and tore his right ACL in one of the most memorable celebration injuries in NFL history.When Cris Collinsworth saw Hutchinson get hurt in an eerily similar fashion, he suggested a ban on at least one aspect of celebrating.“Yeah, if I were a head coach in this league, I would have two main rules,” Collinsworth said. "If you score a touchdown, you're going to run over and hand the ball to the referee. We're not going to have one of those (situations) where you drop it before you get to the goal line, all right?“The second would be if you're celebrating a touchdown, a sack or whatever, it is against the law to leave your feet. No jumping! How many more players are we going to have to see end their career or have a major injury celebrating by jumping and landing in the wrong way? It made me sick today watching Aidan Hutchinson hurt himself after a great play.”___With contributions from AP Sports Writer Stephen Whyno and AP freelancer Dana Gauruder.___See AP’s full NFL coverage here

articles.title: Bruce Springsteen fan club crumbles following singer’s endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed
articles.content: Spring-Nuts, a Bruce Springsteen fan club on Facebook, shut down after the musician endorsed Michigan's Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Howard and Julie Chazanoff, founders of the private fan collective of nearly 20,000 members and themselves observant Jews, had long upheld a "no-politics" policy to encourage "peaceful interactions" among members, the couple wrote in a Nov. 8 post announcing the shuttering. "As Bruce became more outspoken about his politics, something we understood and respected as his absolute right, we found ourselves facing a difficult balancing act," the couple wrote in their lengthy statement, running more than 4,600 words. "So, we decided to modify our no-politics policy and to allow Bruce's political messages and commentary into the group.... We believed that in modifying our no politics policy, and listening to the passionate voices of our members, we were respecting Bruce’s voice and, in our own way, LETTING FREEDOM RING." Posted to his website Nov. 2, Springsteen's endorsement read, "Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution, he’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House. That’s why I’m in his corner 100%." The Chazanoffs said divisions among their large membership over the years had became unmanageable, and Springsteen's most recent political statement hit a nerve. "Most disturbing to us was Bruce's recent endorsement of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has strong relationships with people who have open disdain for America and Jews. El- Sayed refused to retract some of his own statements which we believe to be antisemitic and anti-American," they wrote. "Julie and I were deeply affected by it, too. Not simply as the founders of Spring-Nuts, but on a deeply personal level, as individuals whose principles, convictions, and Jewish identity mean far more to us than any fan group, artist, or political disagreement ever could." The Times reached out to Springsteen's representatives, but did not immediately receive a reply. While supporting Springsteen and others' rights to express their own political opinions, the couple expressed dismay about "disrespectful" fan engagement in the Facebook group. "Although it’s no secret that Julie and I respectfully but vehemently disagree with Bruce’s endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed, particularly given our concerns about El-Sayed’s alignment with some of the individuals he has associated and campaigned with. Obviously, We DO NOT hold Bruce responsible for some of the behavior we've witnessed within this group," they wrote. Reddit user FlyTheW1988 republished the Chazanoffs' full statement following the group's shutdown, prefacing the post with a disclaimer: "Let me be clear, since I’m getting downvoted to oblivion: I didn’t write this and think it’s self-righteousness over the top sanctimonious hot garbage that could have been at most a paragraph. Just sharing in its entirety because I don’t have time to read it let alone cut it down." Facebook user Frank Stefanko in a Nov. 9 post defended the Chazanoffs as true fans whose fan site "shared cultures and enjoyed an international commonality and positive energy." But he took issue with members criticizing the musician for "getting too political," saying it "doesn't compute!" when someone claims to like him "then criticizes the very core of who he is." "Bruce has always been political. Did you never listen to his lyrics. Bruce has a lot to say on many subjects. He’s a poet, he’s an artist, and most importantly, he’s a passionate true American," Stefanko wrote. "I question any Spring-nut member who appreciates Bruce Springsteen and then criticizes his right to practice being an American." Springsteen wrapped his 20-date Land of Hope & Dreams American tour in Minneapolis at the end of March. His album "Streets of Minneapolis" was released Jan. 28.

It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US
articles.description: A panel of global health authorities announced formally Tuesday that the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles, urging public health leaders to step up vaccinations and stop the spread of outbreaks. The determination by the Pan American Health Organization had been expected after 12 continuous months of measles outbreaks in […]
articles.content: Children can receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine, above, after 12 months of age. The United States lost its measles elimination status in mid-November 2026 after more than 25 years. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)A panel of global health authorities announced formally Tuesday that the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles, urging public health leaders to step up vaccinations and stop the spread of outbreaks. The determination by the Pan American Health Organization had been expected after 12 continuous months of measles outbreaks in the country, the first beginning in West Texas in fall 2025, and the most recent surging through Pennsylvania. This year, at least 10 people have died of measles, including two deaths announced last week. Also this week, nearly a dozen scientists with the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention independently published a public health alert noting that at least 112 pregnant women and 13 newborns have been infected with the virus, some with dire outcomes. “Once the measles gets a foothold in a community, it’s very contagious, and can include people who are pregnant,” said Dr. John Gaudet, a retired pediatrician and associate professor at the William Carey University College of Osteopathic Medicine in Mississippi, who was unaffiliated with the public health alert. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus with symptoms that include fever, cough and rash. The disease can cause complications including pneumonia, encephalitis and blindness and can lead to death. But it also can be prevented through a two-dose vaccine known as MMR, or measles, mumps and rubella. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional office of the World Health Organization, concluded in2000 that the U.S. had essentially eliminated measles because spread had been squashed for 12 months or more. After convening last week, a panel of experts at PAHO determined the United States’ “measles elimination status” has been reversed. The organization made the same determination for Bolivia and Mexico. Canada, which lost its status a year ago, was determined to have disrupted transmissions and to be making progress toward regaining elimination status. PAHO noted in its announcement that measles outbreaks can be concentrated in particular communities or geographic regions within a country. “National vaccination figures can mask these disparities, while barriers to health services, missed vaccinations, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy leave children, adolescents and adults vulnerable to infection,” the statement said. In the United States, many public health experts are worried because children, who generally don’t get their first MMR dose until at least one year of age, are highly susceptible, including those who contract the virus before birth. There were 112 confirmed cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles between Jan. 1, 2025, and Sept. 28, 2026, according to the public health alert published Monday in the journal NEJM Evidence. (The authors defined congenital measles as cases transmitted to newborns in utero or with a positive test or febrile rash within 10 days of birth to a woman with confirmed measles.) . All but two of the women had not received the MMR vaccine or had an unknown vaccine status. Quotation I tell them, I’ve never seen the measles, but you will. Be ready. – Dr. John Gaudet, retired pediatrician and associate professor of osteopathic medicine Among the pregnancy cases with reported outcomes, 19 women experienced live births and two lost their pregnancies, the alert said. Of the live births, eight were preterm and eight had to be admitted into the neonatal intensive care unit. Thirteen of those newborns tested positive for congenital measles, and six developed measles-related symptoms, including one infant who showed symptoms related to a life-threatening brain-swelling condition, according to the health alert. The other pregnancy cases either had unknown outcomes or were in women who were still pregnant as of Sept. 28. Gaudet said one of the often-fatal neurological complications of measles known as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, usually shows up between two and 10 years after a measles infection in older children and young adults. But if the infection is contracted in utero, he said, it can happen much earlier. “The whole timeline is compressed if it’s congenital,” Gaudet told Stateline. Infant mortality rates in the United States are high compared with other high-income countries worldwide, with a rate of about 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024-2025, according to provisional CDC data. That rate is more than double among Black infants. “Health care systems and clinicians should be prepared to provide care to pregnant women and their infants with measles, particularly in communities with a high proportion of unvaccinated people,” the health alert said. The United States had 5,412 reported measles cases as of Nov. 12, according to the CDC, more than double the 2,289 cases through all of 2025. Among this year’s cases, nearly 18%, or 951, were among children below the age of 5. Throughout his leadership, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken critic of vaccinations and is opposed to many vaccine mandates, including recommending fewer vaccines for children at the same time that many Republican-led states have ended vaccine mandates for their populations. At least 39 states now have MMR vaccination rates below 95% — the threshold considered necessary for herd immunity. In a statement posted to the social media site X on Tuesday, Kennedy blamed the decline in vaccinations on the COVID-19 pandemic and said that the agency has been responding to measles outbreaks. “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” Kennedy wrote. “Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad,” Kennedy wrote. “CDC has worked alongside state teams in Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control. CDC is also supporting Pennsylvania and New York with epidemiologists and other experts.” “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz, said in a written email statement to Stateline. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Quotation I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles. – U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., in a post on X Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, a group representing local health officials, told Stateline that it’s critical that state health departments are well funded enough to carry out a public health campaign to vaccinate their populations. But without vaccination mandates, she said, pediatricians play a pivotal role in informing parents about the safety and efficacy of the MMR vaccine. “They are the most important because we know in lots of surveys, lots of what we hear on the ground, that providers are the most trusted members of the community, and that one-on-one physician-patient or provider-patient relationship is so important,” Kansagra said. “They’re also the first folks that will see somebody that might walk in that could have measles. And making sure that they have the tools they need to be able to respond appropriately is also really important.” Gaudet said in his three decades as a practicing pediatrician, he never saw a case of measles. But as he teaches medical students, he said he shows them textbook pictures and gives them as much information as he can. “I tell them, ‘I’ve never seen the measles, but you will. Be ready.’” Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org, and reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org. articles.title: Black mothers around US say pregnancy, postpartum needs are often unmet
articles.description: The majority of a group of over 1,600 Black mothers of infants and toddlers across the country said they lacked access to continuous and comprehensive reproductive health care before, during and after pregnancy and have often felt ignored or discriminated by medical professionals, according to a report co-produced and released Tuesday by several groups that […]
articles.content: Affordable childcare advocate Danielle Stewart gets ready for the day with her daughter, Marilyn, on June 15, 2026, at their home in Ladue, Mo. Like many of the 1,600 Black mothers who answered a national survey, Stewart said she wasn’t fully listened to by doctors at the hospital. (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).The majority of a group of over 1,600 Black mothers of infants and toddlers across the country said they lacked access to continuous and comprehensive reproductive health care before, during and after pregnancy and have often felt ignored or discriminated by medical professionals, according to a report co-produced and released Tuesday by several groups that advocate on behalf of women. Many of respondents’ concerns and experiences are related to structural racism and social inequities, said Amani Echols, senior policy analyst for maternal health at the National Partnership for Women & Families. The partnership conducted the survey along with two other advocacy groups, Black Mamas Matter Alliance and MomsRising. Research has shown that Black women face disproportionately high rates of injury and death related to pregnancy and childbirth compared with other racial groups, and that a majority of those deaths are preventable. “The issues that Black moms are experiencing are not due to individual failures or individual behaviors, but a reflection of systemic failures and inequities,” Echols said. “Over and over again, we heard moms share their experiences of disrespectful maternity care where they felt ignored, not listened to, their requests for timely care were not prioritized.” Black mothers reported among their top concerns receiving unwanted labor and birth interventions. About 31% of respondents said they experienced little to no shared decisionmaking around having their pregnancies induced with medication or invasive procedures. Among respondents with a cesarean birth, 63% were unplanned, compared with 46% among white respondents. But the report also points out that within the same group of C-section deliveries, 75% of Black women, a larger percentage than other racial groups, experienced regular labor contractions beforehand, “raising questions about the benefits and necessity of surgery.” “I feel angry about my C-section because it wasn’t the experience I wanted or expected,” reads an anonymous quote in the report. “I felt like the decision was out of my control, and that loss of choice left me frustrated and disappointed. There have been recent reports of Black women forced by court order to have C-sections. One mother with a life-altering birth injury is Danielle Stewart from Missouri, who in 2014 experienced a failed epidural that left her paralyzed from the waist down. “Imagine walking into a hospital to have your first child and leaving on a stretcher alone, paralyzed from your waist down,” Stewart told the Missouri Independent, alleging the anesthesiologist had dismissed her pain concerns. She sued the hospital, which settled, and has since become an advocate for affordable child care. The Listening to Black Mothers survey is the latest in the National Partnership’s ongoing, intermittent Listening to Mothers survey series launched in 2002. This one reached Black mothers 18 and up in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, who answered in-depth questionnaires about their experiences around hospital births in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Among their other top concerns was limited access to family planning. Only 37% of Black respondents intended to become pregnant when they did, compared with 52% of white respondents. Support during pregnancy and labor from doulas and midwives has been linked to better outcomes for Black women and babies. But just 7% received most of their maternity care from midwives, though 73% expressed they would want to consider such care for future pregnancies. About 17% of respondents said they received doula support. Another concern was lack of access to treatment for mental health issues during and after pregnancy, which were high among Black mothers. Among respondents with symptoms of anxiety or depression, 58% said they received no treatment during pregnancy, and 53% said they received no treatment after pregnancy. Relatedly, many Black respondents reported gaps in insurance coverage before, during and after pregnancy. Looming federal Medicaid cuts are expected to disproportionately affect Black families. Among the survey respondents, Medicaid was the primary payer for the prenatal care of 57% of Black respondents, and Medicaid paid for the childbirth of 62% of respondents. The report zooms in on the impact of climate change on Black mothers: 34% of Black mothers reported experiencing a weather-related disaster during pregnancy, with one respondent saying she had no power for two weeks when she was about four months pregnant. And it delves into discrimination faced by Black and multiracial Black mothers. The majority of Black respondents said they felt safer with providers who shared their race, ethnicity or heritage, but only 1 in 4 always had maternity providers who did. Many in the Black community practice self care to deal with the issues they face. The report comes just two weeks after Democrats swept the midterm elections nationwide, with the help of high Black voter turnout in states such as Georgia and throughout the South, ushering in many Black mothers into office. They include Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, Virgin Islands Democratic Gov.-elect Stacey Plaskett and Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton, of Illinois. Echols said she hopes federal and state lawmakers work to enact some of the policies recommended in the report, and that Congress can slow or prevent some of the federal health cuts slated to go into effect early next year. “The number of Black female legislators is a big win for the maternal health space, but also the record number of healthcare professionals and scientists who campaigned on prioritizing healthcare also makes me really optimistic,” Echols said. “I’m also hopeful that there’s an ability to focus on maternal health in a much more expansive way than we have been able to.” Other recommended congressional policies would provide funding to establish racism and discrimination training for maternity care staff, require state Medicaid programs to cover doula and midwifery services, and increase federal support for Medicaid and public health systems. Efforts to expand access to doulas and birth centers to improve Black maternal mortality outcomes are under way in states such as New Jersey and North Carolina. articles.title: San Diego dumps both Flock cameras and smart streetlights
articles.description: 500+ cameras will go dark just 3 years after mayor urged approval.
articles.content: 500+ cameras will go dark just 3 years after mayor urged approval. On Monday evening, San Diego’s city council voted to end its contracts with two surveillance equipment vendors, Flock and Ubicquia. San Diego is one of the largest cities to end its relationship with Flock, the startup with an estimated valuation of $8.3 billion. “We fucking won!” said Lilly Irani of the Transparent and Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology (TRUST) SD Coalition, speaking in her personal capacity. She and her colleagues have been among the loudest critics in recent years. “The national energy creating left and right and center coalitions was the major cause [of the political victory],” she said, noting that it was only last month that one of the council members revoked his support, creating an opening for a political majority to halt the surveillance. That council member, Stephen Whitburn, said in an October press conference that he wanted his fellow citizens to “feel safe.” “If Flock cameras are causing many San Diegans to feel unsafe, then they have lost effectiveness as a public safety tool,” he said at the time. After the Monday vote, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said in a social media post that he “respect[ed] the Council’s decision” and would not veto the move to stop operation of the cameras across the city. Andrew Smith, a spokesperson for Flock, told Ars in an email on Tuesday that the company also “respect[s] the city’s decision.” But Flock isn’t happy about it. “When a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes is removed, public safety moves backward,” Smith wrote. “That has real consequences: cases will take longer to solve, organized retail theft crews will operate with fewer obstacles, a missing child may not be returned home, and victims may wait longer, or indefinitely, for justice.” At Monday’s city council meeting, police representatives said there has been a 20 percent decline in vehicle theft since 2023, with 689 stolen vehicles recovered as a result of the Flock cameras. The vote is a remarkable turnabout from just three years ago, when the mayor and other municipal leaders urged the city council to approve the program. The city’s wholesale rejection of these devices included Ubicquia’s so-called “smart streetlights” that worked in concert with Flock’s AI-driven automatic license plate reader (ALPR) software. This cessation of smart streetlights marks the second time in less than a decade that San Diego has experimented with and then ultimately rejected this technology. At one point, San Diego purchased thousands of smart streetlight systems from a different vendor, GE Current, but a previous mayoral administration shuttered them in 2020. After that, Ubicquia acquired the smart city platform and proposed a newer installation of 500 cameras in 2023 in partnership with Flock—and supported by police—which was installed in 2023. At the time, a local watchdog agency, the City of San Diego Privacy Advisory Board, asked the city council to vote down the plan. One of its board members, Pegah Parsi, wrote on LinkedIn that she is now feeling “vindication.” “A reminder for every city, agency, and institution: if you create an advisory board of experts, listen to them!” she wrote. “Actually, earnestly listen to them. It’s cheaper than learning the hard way. Do better.” That sentiment is echoed by Secure Justice, an Oakland-based advocacy group, which has been studying and monitoring Flock’s issues nationwide. “We’ve documented at least 513 Flock contracts that have ended in red and blue states, in large and small cities,” Brian Hofer, the group’s executive director, emailed Ars. “It’s pretty clear that Americans do not consent to their government tracking them as we go about our daily lives.”

articles.title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
articles.description: Nvidia's interim CEO reaffirmed its open source AI strategy and plans to acquire Hugging Face, despite Jensen Huang's sudden departure.
articles.content: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. “At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months. Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history. The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.” So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call. “Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face. Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.” “That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said. Man gets more than 27 years in US prison for assassination plot that he said was steered from Iran
articles.description: Man gets more than 27 years in US prison for assassination plot that he said was steered from Iran AP News Man sentenced to 27 years in prison over foiled plot to kill Trump The Washington Post Man convicted in Iran-backed plot to murder Trump gets 27.5 years in prison CBS News Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump BBC Pakistani man gets 27 years for foiled plot to kill Trump, Biden D
articles.content: NEW YORK (AP) — A man who admitted trying to get a U.S. politician killed — and said Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard drove him to it — was sentenced Tuesday to nearly three decades in prison. Asif Merchant, a Pakistani businessman, had faced the possibility of life in prison for what the judge called an exceptionally serious crime. Possible targets of the thwarted plot included then-candidate and now-President Donald Trump, then-President Joe Biden or then-candidate and former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, according to trial testimony. “Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a U.S. president or other senior government official,” said U.S. District Judge Eric Komitee, a Trump appointee. Merchant, 48, shifted in his chair but otherwise showed no visible reaction when he was sentenced to a little more than 27 years. One of his lawyers, Avraham Moskowitz, said after court that Merchant plans to appeal but was grateful that the judge turned down prosecutors’ bid for a life term. “I think what it shows is that our judiciary remains independent, thankfully,” Moskowitz said. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that Merchant was “justly sentenced.” The sentencing capped a remarkable trial about an alleged Iran-driven plan to kill a prominent U.S. political figure in the thick of the 2024 campaign season. The Iranian government has denied trying to kill U.S. officials. Merchant, who was convicted earlier this year of murder for hire and attempted terrorism, declined to speak at his sentencing. But at his trial, he bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally, using objects on a hotel napkin to illustrate the scenario for an acquaintance. Merchant then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he’d borrowed from a relative. He testified that he was just playing along with instructions from a Revolutionary Guard intelligence operative in order to protect relatives in Iran. Merchant said he figured that U.S. authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward. U.S. law enforcement was, indeed, onto him: The supposed killers-for-hire actually were undercover FBI agents, tipped by the acquaintance who saw Merchant’s napkin demonstration. Merchant was arrested in Texas while packing for a flight back to Pakistan on July 12, 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump’s life in Butler, Pennsylvania. “This plot was incompetent from the very beginning,” defense lawyer Christopher Neff said in court on Tuesday. “Mr. Merchant’s participation was half-hearted.” Merchant worked for Pakistani banks for decades and then got into businesses ranging from car sales to banana exports, and he traveled periodically to the U.S. for work and to see relatives. He also traveled to Iran for Shiite Muslim religious pilgrimages and visits with kin. After meeting a Revolutionary Guard operative several years ago, Merchant imagined intelligence work would be exciting and profitable, and he feared for his relatives’ safety if he defied the powerful paramilitary, according to his defense. “My family was under threat, and I had to do this,” Merchant testified in March. He said his handler named Biden, Haley and Trump as potential targets. Prosecutors challenged Merchant’s claim that he acted under duress. They noted that he had shared anti-American and anti-Trump social media posts after the U.S. killing of top Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani in 2020, during Trump’s first administration. Merchant’s defense portrayed the posts as venting, and Neff insisted that his client wasn’t an extremist or inclined to turn his beliefs into violence. But Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarah Winik countered that Merchant did “the most extreme thing you can do: Plot the assassination of a government official.” The judge said he believed Merchant had some concern for his family but also was “highly motivated to do harm to this country.”

articles.title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
articles.description: "Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most."
articles.content: Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe's first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company. The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio's shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.Read full article Comments
