articles.content: A digitally-colorized, thin-section transmission electron microscopic image shows a single measles virus particle, with the viral nucleocapsid situated underneath the viral envelope, surrounded by surface projections.(Cynthia S. Goldsmith; William Bellini, Ph.D. / U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)A west Michigan health department has confirmed a measles outbreak for St. Joseph and Hillsdale counties.Twelve people have come down with measles since the outbreak started, according to the Branch-Hillsdale-St. Joseph Community Health Agency. Six are in Hillsdale county and six are in St. Joseph County.“We encourage everyone to take a few minutes to check their vaccination records,” said Rebecca Burns, the agency's health officer. “Making sure you and your family are protected is an important step in preventing the spread of measles.”The outbreak comes as an international health agency announced Tuesday that the U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status, as cases rise at the fastest rate in 30 years.The southwest Michigan health department is encouraging people to check their measles vaccination status, and get the vaccine if they haven’t.The agency is offering vaccination clinics on:Thursday, November 1910 a.m - 6 p.m. at 1555 E. Chicago Road, Sturgis2 p.m. - 5 p.m. at 13751 Tripp Road, WaldronMonday, November 239 a.m. - 5 p.m. at 570 N. Marshall Road, ColdwaterBurns said people can also get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine during normal business hours at the health clinics, or at their doctor’s office.“It’s really widely available,” Burns said of the vaccine.She noted that all of the confirmed cases in Hillsdale and St. Joseph counties affected people who were either unvaccinated or only had one round of the vaccine. She said getting both rounds of the MMR vaccine is 97% effective against the disease, and can help stop the outbreak from spreading further.The community health agency said measles symptoms can include:a high fevercoughrunny nosered eyestiny white spots in the mouthA red, raised, rash that starts on face, spreads to the bodyLast week, the agency confirmed two exposure sites for the outbreak, one at the Three Rivers Health Emergency waiting area on November 5, and another at WellNow urgent care in Sturgis.Burns said investigations for the 12 confirmed cases across Hillsdale and St. Joseph counties are still ongoing, and there may be other cases in the community.

articles.title: Kalamazoo psych hospital had no doctors, state says. Closing it would leave a gap
articles.description: The 64-bed Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital’s documented problems show the friction between Michigan’s mental health needs and its ability to deliver safe services.
articles.content: Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital could lose its license after state regulators found no doctor on site and repeated patient injuries Losing the hospital’s adult psychiatric beds would cut into southwest Michigan’s limited inpatient capacity New developments are attempting to bridge the gap in Michigan’s mental healthcare, but capacity issues remain The possible closure of a southwest Michigan psychiatric hospital is dredging up fresh concerns about how the state can expand mental health services without sacrificing patient safety. The Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital may be shuttered after it was flagged by state and federal regulators over several noncompliance issues and patient complaints, including lacking doctors on site and a pattern of patient injuries. The 64-bed inpatient facility opened in late 2024, according to WOOD-TV, and has been dogged by complaints ever since. The Kalamazoo site is owned by South Bend-based NeuroPsychiatric Hospitals, which also operates behavioral healthcare locations in Indiana, Ohio, Texas and Arizona, according to its website. The company says about half of the Kalamazoo hospital’s beds are reserved for patients with developmental disabilities. The Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs issued a notice to revoke the hospital’s license with a hearing scheduled in December, according to News Channel 3. Related: Michigan boosts bed capacity in ‘horribly underserved’ mental health system Michigan kids in mental health crisis sent out of state as facilities close Mental health advocates optimistic about Michigan reforms With 31 licensed psychiatric beds for adults, Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital represents about 1 in 6 of the adult psychiatric beds available in southwest Michigan. Without the hospital, the eight-county region would have 161 licensed adult psychiatric beds, down from 192. Michigan had about 2,500 licensed adult psychiatric beds, according to the state’s Nov. 1 inventory report, and 360 for children. The lack of service in and around Kalamazoo has been a concern for local lawmakers, who had initially written to delay the state’s decision against the psychiatric hospital. “At the time of our original letter, we asked for additional information so we could better understand the circumstances surrounding this action. Based on the additional information we have now received, we are rescinding our request that the timeline be extended for [Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital],” said state Rep. Julie Rogers, D-Kalamazoo, in a statement. Donate State Rep. Matt Longjohn, D-Portage, a physician who had joined in Rogers’ original request, wrote that while Michigan needs more psychiatric beds, “patient safety must come first.” Bed shortage Michigan’s lack of psychiatric bed capacity has been an ongoing concern for families, patient advocates and law enforcement. The state has taken steps to address the gap, welcoming new developments in Lansing, Grand Rapids and Madison Heights. MyMichigan Health is modernizing its inpatient behavioral health unit through a $22 million construction project in Sault Ste. Marie supported by $3.6 million in state grants. The Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville Township opened in October to replace state-run facilities that opened decades ago. (Eli Newman/Bridge Michigan) The $383 million Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital opened its doors last month as a state-run facility. The 264-bed facility in Northville Township is replacing the Hawthorn Center and Walter Reuther Psychiatric Hospital. The state has about 300 patients on its psychiatric bed wait list, according to Dr. George Mellos, senior deputy director for the State Hospitals Administration. He said assertive community treatment for adults and wraparound services for children are “a direction we need to go” in delivering mental healthcare. “We want people to stay in the community,” Mellos told Bridge in October. “We don’t want people in state hospitals.” Safety concerns From January through May, patients at Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital were sent to other hospitals 43 times for falls, assaults, unexplained injuries or being found unresponsive, according to a LARA letter obtained by News Channel 3. The agency found an assortment of other issues during its investigation on site. There was no psychiatrist or other physician at the facility, according to the report, with nurse practitioners filling the role of treating patients. Inspectors wrote the hospital used paper records in lieu of electronic ones, and the facility “failed to demonstrate providing a safe environment to receive mental health services.” The hospital’s plan to fix the problems fell short, regulators wrote, in part because it didn’t commit to hiring a doctor and because its goal of 90% complete documentation was “not acceptable” for a facility with so many patient injuries. Kalamazoo Behavioral Health Hospital and NeuroPsychiatric Hospitals did not return Bridge Michigan’s request for comment in time for publication. The federal government is taking its own actions. On Monday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ended its Medicare agreement with the hospital after finding the facility failed to meet several standards on patients’ rights, nursing services, physical environment, special medical record requirements for psychiatric hospitals and special staff requirements for psychiatric hospitals.

Black politicians win newfound power across state, federal governments
articles.description: Black politicians will wield unprecedented amounts of power following this month’s seismic midterm elections. Black representation will reach new heights across state and federal governments: In Washington, the U.S. House is set to seat its first Black speaker and the U.S. Senate will include a record seven Black members. Black leaders also set new levels […]
articles.content: Georgia House speaker-nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Democrat, speaks at a news conference on Nov. 12 at the state Capitol in Atlanta announcing the caucus’ picks for leadership roles. Black politicians will wield unprecedented levels of power following this month’s midterm elections. (Photo by Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder)Black politicians will wield unprecedented amounts of power following this month’s seismic midterm elections. Black representation will reach new heights across state and federal governments: In Washington, the U.S. House is set to seat its first Black speaker and the U.S. Senate will include a record seven Black members. Black leaders also set new levels for state representation, according to an analysis by The Collective Political Action Committee, which works to build Black political power by increasing Black representation in state and local governments. A record five states and the U.S. Virgin Islands will be led by Black governors. And voters are poised to send a record nine Black lieutenant governors, eight Black attorneys general and nine Black state House speakers to office in 2027. “Now, you’re actually going to see Black leaders in positions to drive policy, to determine what policy issues get debated, what policy issues get attention, and also what policy issues get covered by the media,” said Quentin James, founder and president of The Collective PAC. In total, the political action committee expects between 850 and 900 Black lawmakers in state capitols next year once election results are finalized. That’s poised to set a record and represent more than 11% of the nation’s 7,386 state lawmakers. “For one election cycle to do what we haven’t done in 250 years, I think it’s more than historic,” James said. “It is kind of a cultural shift in terms of what it means to now be a Black elected official.” Not every legislative chamber has selected leaders for upcoming sessions. But so far state House chambers in Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Maryland, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and Virginia are expected to be led by Black speakers. In Illinois, embattled House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch recently announced he would not seek another term leading the chamber. Citing unnamed sources, FOX Chicago recently reported that the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus would only support one of its own members as successor. That means as many as 10 state Houses could be led by Black speakers next year. After flipping control of the lower chamber, Georgia House Democrats last week nominated Rep. Carolyn Hugley for House speaker. If approved by the full House, she would become Georgia’s first Black speaker. In a news conference, Hugley described the new Democratic leadership as “a team that looks like Georgia.” In Georgia, Black women will hold at least nine statewide executive offices — up from one currently. Nationally, Black women will hold at least 19 statewide executive offices, according to The Collective PAC. The number of Black lieutenant governors is expected to nearly double from five to nine. In Kansas, Oklahoma, New York and South Carolina, voters elected their state’s first ever Black lieutenant governors. As with the record number of women elected this year, the rise in Black representation was largely driven by Democratic gains. In Florida, Byron Donalds will become the state’s first Black governor and the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor. Following the midterms, only one Black Republican will serve in Congress, U.S. Sen. Tim Scott, of South Carolina. James said Black Republicans such as Donalds and Scott have a chance at recasting what it means to be a Black Republican in the post-Trump era. While his organization works to elect Black Democrats, he said it’s important to have representation on both sides of the aisle. “That’s a way where we could find more political equity,” he said, “because yes, there are African Americans who are conservative. They should be represented as well. But I don’t think the MAGA movement is the best place for that representation to occur on the right.” Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
articles.description: Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.
articles.content: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.Read full article Comments

Governor Hochul and Mayor Mamdani Announce Groundbreaking on Affordable and Supportive Housing and Community Facility in Astoria
articles.content: Governor Kathy Hochul, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Borough President Donovan Richards Jr., and Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens President and CEO Costa Constantinides were on hand on November 17 along with other elected officials for the groundbreaking for the redevelopment of the Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens. Upon completion, the site will be the largest Boys and Girls Club facility in the nation. Governor Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on November 17 the groundbreaking for the redevelopment of the Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens. The $320 million redevelopment project consists of replacing the outdated original build­ing with a new 14-story mixed-use building featuring 236 affordable homes, space for youth services and community amenities such as a new planetarium, theater, arena, and a charter school. Upon completion, the site will be the largest Boys and Girls Club facility in the nation. “As we build a more affordable and livable New York, adding new, high-quality hous­ing is a top priority for my administration and we won’t leave any stone unturned,” Gov­ernor Hochul said. “Beyond delivering affordable and supportive housing that hundreds of New Yorkers will soon call home, this space will allow families to enjoy so much right from the comfort of their homes. Whether sending their kids to school, seeing a play in the new theater, or staying active at the fitness center, this new facility is going to make a real difference for New York fami­lies.” Rendering of the interior of the new VBGCQ building. New York City Mayor Zohran K. Mam­dani said, “For close to a century, the Vari­ety Boys and Girls Club has been an anchor in Astoria. Today’s groundbreaking is a spe­cial day, not only because this new facility will host amenities like a planetarium, pool and mental health facility, but because we are building 236 affordable homes where New Yorkers can live with dignity and sta­bility. Thank you to Governor Hochul and every leader who made this moment possi­ble.” The redevelopment project began with the demolition of Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens’ original clubhouse, which was built in 1955 and no longer capable of meeting current demands. The new 138,000 square foot facility will be large enough to serve 16,000 families annually – 11,000 more than the previous facility – and in­clude after-school and teen programming, aquatics, athletics, arts, and STEM learn­ing. The 236-unit residential portion of the building, known as ICL-Variety Residences at Astoria, will be affordable to households earning up to 80 percent of the Area Media Income. And in keeping with the larger re­development project’s mission of pairing affordable housing with community pro­gramming for all ages, there will be 71 sup­portive housing units reserved for eligible young adults who are experiencing or at-risk of homelessness, including those who left foster care. Seventeen apartments will be fully-accessible, with twelve adapted for residents with mobility disabilities, and five adapted for residents with sensory disabili­ties. Residents of the facility will have ac­cess to a community room and fitness cen­ter. The project will also include a 1,500-seat arena, a planetarium, 2,700 square foot retail space, incubator space for businesses and nonprofits, theater, indoor pool, and hockey rink. There will be educa­tional space set aside for STEM, robotics, arts, music, dance, and media classes. The redevelopment will also include a 432-stu­dent charter school. The project is developed by Mega, In­stitute for Community Living (ICL), and Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens. ICL is also providing the on-site support serv­ices for the 71 supportive apartments. The all-electric building will feature ge­othermal heating, rooftop solar panels, an energy recovery ventilation system to en­hance indoor air quality, ENERGY STAR appliances, and LED lighting. Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens President and CEO Costa Constantinides said, “For more than 70 years, Variety has been a place where Queens kids find safety, belonging and the confidence to pursue what comes next. This campus brings learn­ing, play, the arts and housing together so more young people can discover their pas­sions and build their futures. We are invest­ing in the next generation and in the institution that will be here to support them.” Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. said, “There has been no greater example of youth empowerment, public safety and community development than the Variety Boys and Girls Club of Queens’ clubhouse in Astoria. Countless families have been strengthened by Vari­ety’s programming, but as the need for its services grows, so must its physical foot­print. I couldn’t be prouder to have allo­cated $10 million toward the construction of Variety’s incredible new clubhouse, as we build the largest Boys and Girls club­house in the nation right here in The World’s Borough. From its history-making planetarium and extensive educational re­sources to its hundreds of units of afford­able housing for neighbors who need it most, I know this community center will change countless lives for decades to come.” Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas said, “For generations, Variety Boys & Girls Club has been a second home to young people across Western Queens, giv­ing them opportunities to learn, grow, and build a future for themselves. Today, we are investing in that legacy and making sure it can reach even more families. This project is about so much more than a new club­house. With expanded educational and ath­letic programming, a dedicated children’s development center, and affordable housing that will provide stability for young people aging out of foster care, we are creating re­sources that our community needs and de­serves. I am proud to celebrate this milestone and look forward to seeing the next generation of Queens children benefit from this investment.” Assemblymember Steven Raga said, “Every young person deserves a safe, wel­coming place to learn, play, and pursue their potential. I thank Governor Hochul for her steadfast commitment to our youth and Queens families, and congratulate Variety Boys & Girls Club of Queens for advancing this vital project. This groundbreaking brings us closer to expanded educational and recreational opportunities for thousands of young people, alongside critically needed affordable housing that will help New Yorkers remain in the neighborhoods they call home.” Error loading comments: ' + (response.data || 'Unknown error') + ' Error loading comments. articles.title: Who speaks for the trees? As housing fights roil Michigan, it’s the residents
articles.description: In Sterling Heights, a new housing development was going to put at risk the life of a Chinkapin oak tree, estimated to be more than 250 years old. Now, the city is keeping the land the tree is on, but advocates are still worried about it and some other trees
articles.content: Some Sterling Heights residents pushed back when they learned a development could mean the end of an a centuries-old oak tree Now, the land the tree is on will be spared but advocates still worry for it and more than 100 other trees Development pressures may mean that either trees in cities or trees in rural areas will be cut STERLING HEIGHTS — An oak tree stands here on a wooded lot with a red, white and blue ribbon dangling from its waist. Nearby, a sign declares: “This tree is older than the nation!” And for the past two years, it’s also been the subject of intense debate in Sterling Heights, where preservationists clashed with officials poised to sell the plot the tree sits on to pave the way for new affordable housing. For now, at least, demands to save the tree have won. The City Council voted this month to hold onto the small circle of land beneath the oak. It will still sell the surrounding plot for a smaller development with pricier “workforce housing” units. The tree is a chinkapin oak, admired for its chestnut-like leaves and appreciated by wildlife for its acorns. The species can live to be 300 to 400 years old, and experts estimate this one has already surpassed 250. “It has these unique leaves (that) look kind of like little saw blades,” Mark Graf told Bridge Michigan as he picked one up, pointing to its serrated edges. Sterling Heights resident Mark Graf helped lead an effort to save this centuries-old chinkapin oak tree from development in his city. But Graf still worries about this tree and others slated to be cut down. (Laura Herberg/Bridge Michigan) Graf was among the residents who led the charge to save the tree, arguing it was an irreplaceable green gem in the concrete-heavy Detroit suburb, which has grown to be the fourth-largest city in the state and is nearly fully developed. Officials listened, but some advocates are still worried and unsatisfied, fearing the development may ultimately damage or even kill the tree. Related: Michigan Big Tree Hunt finds a whopper: A weeping willow, 327 inches around A sequoia forest in Detroit? Planting world’s largest trees on vacant lots Michigan restricts buckthorn, other plants as landscapers cry foul Similar battles have played out across the state as sprawl and development encroach upon trees that have grown for decades or even centuries. Earlier this year, Kalamazoo residents blocked a wooded area from being converted to a commercial development. In 2023, Huron Township residents called the local news when a housing developer began cutting down the forest near their homes. And last year, Gaylord residents went haywire when it seemed like trees might be cut down for solar panels.Donate In the case of Sterling Heights, the tree “has been the celebrity, but it’s not the whole story,” Graf said. Tree City USA Sterling Heights, which Arbor Day Foundation has recognized dozens of times for its annual Tree City USA program, bought the property where the oak tree stands using federal stimulus funding from the American Rescue Plan Act. The city, with a population of roughly 134,000 residents, spent $1 million of its $20 million in COVID-19 recovery funds to create “micro-forests” throughout the suburb. Mayor Michael Taylor described it as a response to developers who had built out “every nook and cranny of the community,” clearing trees in the process. This chinkakin oak tree in Sterling Heights is believed to be at least 250 years old – the age of the United States. (Laura Herberg/Bridge Michigan) Sterling Heights also has a tax-funded initiative to preserve green space and reforest the city’s tree canopy, so some residents were surprised when officials issued a request for proposals to develop the property with the chinkapin oak, at Van Dyke near M-59. But officials say the demand for housing is real, too, projecting the city will need to add up to 2,100 housing units over the next decade to accommodate anticipated growth. As of this spring, City Development Director Jason Castor estimated that between 18% and 23% of Sterling Heights was covered by tree canopy, well short of its 40% goal. A site map of a planned development in Sterling Heights shows the proposed building in the bottom right, the chinkapin oak to the left of that, and land subject to excavation where trees will be cut down and replanted with graphing squares. The three clusters of white land, primarily wetland, is not currently slated to be touched. (Courtesy of Sterling Heights) Statewide, about 55% of Michigan is forested, but canopy coverage drops to an average of about 30% in urban communities and is declining. Parts of Sterling Heights have less than 10% tree cover, according to an analysis by American Forests, a national nonprofit that analyzes satellite imagery to estimate canopy. The chinkapin oak sits in an area with 32% coverage, among the lushest in the city. Trees are important for cities like Sterling Heights because they provide shade and stormwater management and other benefits, said Richard Norton, professor of urban and regional planning with the University of Michigan. Sign up for our outdoors newsletter Want more coverage like this delivered directly into your inbox? Sign up for the Bridge Michigan Outdoors newsletter here. But it can be a challenge for cities with growing populations to preserve larger, older trees, he noted. “You want to protect them, but at the same time, you don’t want to just rope off the city and say, ‘No more development because we’re saving our trees,’ and now you’re pushing development out into ecologically important rural exurb areas,” Norton said. Those more rural areas are often where more wildlife and critters live, he said, which is why cities are “where growth and development should go.” ‘Remember this day’ The chinkapin oak sits on a 10-acre site that is adjacent to the Clinton River and is subject to flooding. It once housed an amusement park but is now a green space that could be mistaken for an underdeveloped park. The grass is mowed around a few of the bigger trees, including the chinkapin. There’s a wooded brush area away from the road, near the river. The Chaldean Community Foundation won the initial bid to develop the land, proposing an affordable housing complex with retail space on the bottom level. When residents saw the plans, some realized they could be losing a centuries-old tree. They began to show up at public meetings and promoted an online petition that around 4,000 people have signed. A rendering of the building that the Chaldean Community Foundation plans to build at 43934 Van Dyke Ave., Sterling Heights. The chinkapin oak that was once slated to be cut down, but will now be spared, is located to the left of the building. (Courtesy of Sterling Heights) The foundation ultimately changed its plans, designing a smaller building without retail and with fewer but pricier “workforce housing” units. The updated design, foundation and city officials said, would spare the old oak tree. But some residents are still concerned the chinkapin could be knocked over, flooded out or have its roots compacted by heavy machinery used during construction or plans to create a gathering space around the tree. “I want you to remember this day,” Lisa Graf, Mark Graf’s wife, told members of the Sterling Heights City Council this month in a public hearing. “In five years or 10 years, should you vote ‘yes’ to develop this property, when you see the tree die, (know that) your decision affected that.” The reimagined housing project will still need to go through site plan and engineering reviews. Because the property contains small pockets of wetlands, it may require approval by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy. Some brush and woods behind a chinkapin oak tree in Sterling Heights that is more than 250 years old. The area is slated for development and many trees, but not this oak, will be cut down and replaced with new trees. (Laura Herberg/Bridge Michigan) Planting replacements It’s not just the chinkapin that local residents are concerned about. It’s estimated that 114 of the 284 trees on the property will need to be removed for the development, according to an initial review cited by City Planner Jake Parcell. Of those, 21 are large enough to meet the city’s definition of landmark trees, which would require developers to plant 331 replacements. “Every single person that lives anywhere, every single person who is a person, lives somewhere where a tree used to be,” Taylor, the mayor, said during public debate. “Trees are a renewable resource. We can always keep planting trees.” But some research has shown that in order to compensate for cutting down one large tree, you’d need to plant up to 41 new trees. Curious how many trees are in your urban area? You can search for a neighborhood’s tree canopy percentage using this interactive map. SOURCE: American Forests Councilmember Maria Schmidt said having the property be “reforested with very small trees that will take a very long time to come to maturity” felt hypocritical because the city recently asked its voters to pay more to preserve green spaces. Graf, standing near the chinkapin oak, looked at the nearby trees that may still be removed and thought about the smaller trees that developers would plant in their place. “You look at what all these trees are doing now, and it’s going to be decades, even a century into the future before any of those trees, if they survive, even start to do that,” he said. Not too long after, a bald eagle flew out of the woods and landed on a tall tree not far from the old oak.

articles.title: New Shelby Twp. playground marks start of Activities Center expansion
articles.content: The opening of a $379,000 playground is only just the beginning for new facilities at the Shelby Township Activities Center. The playground is a modest first step of a planned $3.5-million expansion of the Activities Center, located on 21 Mile west of Hayes Road, that will start next year with preconstruction work, according to the township. Officials marked the opening of the playground with a Nov. 9 ribbon-cutting ceremony. Township leaders said the new play equipment gives youngsters and their families a new outdoor space to play and enjoy on top of the existing facilities at the center. “The place is amazing it makes you wish you were a kid again,” said Michael Weatherly in reply to a Facebook post about the opening. “Today, we open the new playground to support the families that use the facility after 5 p.m. every day and in the summer as part of our Summer Recreation Day Camp,” township Supervisor Richard Stathakis said. “Our residents have told us loud and clear through their participation in programs here, our annual community visioning survey, and by stopping me on the street that the Activities Center needs more, and we’re listening and acting on that feedback.” The exterior property currently includes outdoor pickleball courts, a pavilion, softball diamond and the Shelby Township Community Garden. Phase two will add approximately 13,440-square-feet to the 25,000-square-foot facility, including a new gymnasium, an indoor walking track and additional pickleball courts in an effort to meet a growing demand for recreational offerings, officials said. The project was originally slated to cost $2.1 million and be completed by the end of 2025. But officials increased the scope and price tag. “After further review with and feedback from the senior center members it was determined to move forward with the more robust plan which expanded the budget to $3.5 million,” said township spokesman Brad Bates. The project is supported by a $1.5 million federal Community Project Funding grant that was secured two over two years ago by U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township. “These and all of our improvements are paid in cash with no debt, no bonding, and no increase in taxes, so we’re saving the funds we need to complete that activities center expansion without increasing the debt burden for our residents and taxpayers,” Stathakis said. Stathakis commended Parks, Recreation and Maintenance Director Joe Youngblood for his “amazing job expanding our parks and recreation programs with the Activities Center that, in just seven years of operation, it already needs to expand.” “When we opened the new senior center in the Activities Center, we really wanted to focus on space and programs to keep our seniors active, and they’ve responded with more participation than I ever could have dreamed of,” Youngblood said. “Our senior center membership is higher than it’s ever been, and they love programs like our pickleball, senior aerobics and other activities to keep moving, so phase two will help us meet that growing demand.” The Activites Center was created by the township spending $3.75 million to purchase and transform the former Boys & Girls Club in 2019 to serve as the home of the Senior Center, Parks, Recreation and Maintenance Department offices, and a community activities center. The township expanded the center’s property with the purchase of 1.7 acres in 2022. The Activities Center replaced the old senior center on Van Dyke north of 23 Mile Road. In July, officials broke ground on construction of an $11-million amphitheater and community relations building behind the Shelby Township Hall at 52700 Van Dyke Avenue, just south of 24 Mile Road. The amphitheater project replaces the old bandshell, which was demolished in 2019 to make way for the new public library. The new 20,000-square-foot facility will be paid for in cash, officials said.

articles.title: Lawrence among newly elected progressives doubling down on calls for federal data center moratorium
articles.description: Outside of the U.S. Capitol building, standing behind stacks of bankers boxes, a number of progressive representatives gathered with labor advocates, political organizers and environmentalists to demand a pause on data center development until regulations can be put in place. During a Tuesday press conference, Jim Walsh, the policy director for Food & Water Watch […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) joins organizers, labor advocates and environmentalists in Washington, D.C. demanding a federal data center moratorium on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo Courtesy of Food and Water Watch)Outside of the U.S. Capitol building, standing behind stacks of bankers boxes, a number of progressive representatives gathered with labor advocates, political organizers and environmentalists to demand a pause on data center development until regulations can be put in place. During a Tuesday press conference, Jim Walsh, the policy director for Food & Water Watch said they intended to deliver 250,000 petitions to Congress seeking immediate action on a federal data center moratorium. “The American public resoundingly rejected data centers two weeks ago, and Congress needs to follow their lead,” Walsh said, “Hundreds of organizations, hundreds of communities across the country, hundreds of thousands of people and millions of voters are saying no to data centers.” The buildout of data centers – facilities that house servers and technology needed to power the internet and develop artificial intelligence tools – has become a flashpoint issue for communities throughout the country. Michigan is no exception, as an ever-growing number of data center proposals bucks up against community concerns of how these resource-demanding facilities will impact their electricity rates, their access to drinking water, and the state’s ability to meet its 100% clean energy standard by 2040. U.S. Rep. James McGovern (D-Massachusetts), who is among the lead sponsors of the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act introduced by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), argued that the White House is asleep at the wheel when it comes to AI policy, calling for an immediate change to the status quo. Will Lawrence rolls out plan for regulating Big Tech, data centers in Michigan and beyond “People are sick of big, powerful tech companies squashing competition, controlling how we use the internet and driving up prices for everyday people,” McGovern said. “They want us to fight back, and they want us to take action immediately. The American people are done getting screwed over by unelected, unaccountable big tech oligarchs.” McGovern also questioned the tactics data center developers have used to advance projects in American communities. “Let’s get real, if this AI infrastructure is so great, why are they making shady deals without community input,” McGovern asked. “If it is so profitable, why are they begging for government subsidies? And if it’s so popular, why are the voices of people so loud begging them to stop?” “And I’m going to tell you why,” McGovern continued. “Because they’re lying.” With Democrats set to take control of the Republican-led U.S. House and U.S. Senate in the new year, McGovern said change is coming, and that they would reassert Congress’s power over the issues that matter to the American people. Among the incoming members of Democrats’ newly won majority is U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence of Lansing, who defeated U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Lawrence made data centers and accountability for tech companies a cornerstone of his campaign, calling for a moratorium on both data center and advanced AI development. “This was not an issue that was on many of our radars, you know, 15 months ago, and it wasn’t mine, but I’m trained as an organizer. As an organizer, the first thing you learn is to listen,” Lawrence said, noting that his district has seen several hyperscale data centers proposed over the past year and a half. “I’m not somebody who, you know, thinks that there’s no potential use for AI,” Lawrence said. “I mean, it’s a marvelous technology. It’s the sum distillation of human language that now has been trained to talk back to us, and it is capable of amazing things. Maybe we could make medical advances and things of this nature.” However, Lawrence stressed that in its current form, AI technology is not being built in service of the people. “We know for certain that under the current incentives, it is going to be used to put people out of work, to harm the environment, to undermine our democracy, and to put us all at terrible risk,” Lawrence said, reiterating his support for a moratorium.

articles.title: Claims by Netanyahu’s party of a ‘stolen’ Israeli election unravel
articles.description: Claims by Netanyahu’s party of a ‘stolen’ Israeli election unravel AP News Netanyahu’s opponents demand investigation after report alleges that his staff tried to influence elections CNN Eisenkot condemns Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens The Guardian Source of vote-buying claims quit PM’s office after posing as security official – reports The Times of Israel Source behind Arab activists' a
articles.content: NAHARIYA, Israel (AP) — Since suffering heavy losses in Israel’s Oct. 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party has repeatedly claimed the vote was “stolen” by Arab-led parties, possibly with foreign assistance. Those claims appear to be crumbling as the longest-serving Israeli leader tries to cling to power. Israeli authorities say they have found no evidence to support the Likud party’s claims. And in a new setback to Netanyahu, Israel’s attorney general is looking into revelations that unsubstantiated claims of voter bribery originated with Netanyahu’s own staff. There are no signs Netanyahu was personally involved in wrongdoing. But his party’s unsuccessful attempts to discredit the election have left him in a weakened position as his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, moves ahead with efforts to form a new government and oust Netanyahu. Early on the morning of the election, Israeli police announced the arrests of three suspects in a Bedouin Arab town and said they had confiscated envelopes filled with cash. They said the men were suspected of paying people to vote for the Arab-led Ra’am party. Netanyahu immediately jumped on the announcement, calling it a “serious incident” and demanding a police investigation. Four additional suspects were arrested days later, and the incident would become a cornerstone of the Likud party’s campaign to discredit the vote, in which Arab-led parties posted strong gains in representation, jumping from 15 seats to 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. But the accusations quickly fell apart. A judge ordered all of the men released within days due to a lack of evidence, and none were charged. On Tuesday, after meeting with Israel’s internal security service, the Shin Bet, the country’s Election Committee said “there is no evidence that bribes were paid to voters on a scale that could have affected the election results.” The committee said its investigation is ongoing but shifting to examine allegations of foreign influence, another Likud claim. In the past few days, signs have emerged that the unsubstantiated allegations against Arab voters can be traced directly to Netanyahu’s office and allies. The information appears to have originated with Danny Greenberg, a former adviser to the prime minister on Arab affairs. Greenberg told Israel’s Yediot Ahronoth newspaper that he received a tip from a member of the Arab-led Joint List party whom he declined to identify. He said he then passed information to Netanyahu’s chief of staff. Earlier this week, Netanyahu’s office said the chief of staff, Ido Norden, was “doing his duty as a law-abiding Israeli citizen” by reporting a possible crime to police. He said his office had no further involvement. Israel’s police commissioner said Monday he would investigate the police handling of the affair. But late Monday, Israel’s attorney general ordered police to freeze the probe. Instead, she said she will hold discussions about a broader investigation, including a look at the communications between Netanyahu’s office and police close to election day. Netanyahu’s bloc of religious and nationalist parties lost its parliamentary majority in the election, but Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister. The latest developments come at a bad time for him. In a possible first step toward unseating Netanyahu, Eisenkot’s allies installed their own parliament speaker on Tuesday. That clears the way for Eisenkot to reverse some of Netanyahu’s more controversial policies while he continues to try to cobble together a majority coalition in the Knesset. Eisenkot faces his own struggles because he may be forced to rely on Arab-led parties, a potentially risky move. Netanyahu has sought to head off any alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties, pejoratively referring to them as “terror supporters.” Instead, he has called on Eisenkot to join him in a government under Netanyahu’s leadership. Eisenkot said this week that the actions of Netanyahu and his inner circle pose a “tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy.” Yoav Dotan, a law professor at Hebrew University, said the Likud party’s attempts to discredit the vote were part of a larger pattern. Netanyahu has frequently made incendiary statements against Arab voters during elections. “It’s not surprising, because it’s not a bug, it’s a feature in his strategy during this election,” Dotan said. “The only point that might surprise someone is that it was pretty clumsy.”

articles.title: Experts: Make these 5 plants illegal to buy in Michigan
articles.description: Experts with the Michigan Invasive Species Program are recommending the state add five plants to its invasive species list. Officials will vote on the draft order at a later date.
articles.content: Under a draft order, Michigan would prohibit or restrict five plants: creeping water-primrose, large flowered water-primrose, common butterbur, lesser celandine and round-leaf bittersweet If added to the invasive species list, these plants could not be brought into or sold in the state People can submit public comments on the draft order between Wednesday and Dec. 18 Five additional plants could eventually be restricted or prohibited in Michigan. Members of the state’s Invasive Species Program are recommending action to combat the non-native species likely to cause harm to the environment. Under a draft order introduced Tuesday, Michigan would add creeping water-primrose, large flowered water-primrose, common butterbur, lesser celandine and round-leaf bittersweet to its list of prohibited or restricted invasive species. If approved by the Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development, it would be illegal for the plants to be introduced, sold, traded, moved or shared in Michigan, though existing plants could remain in the ground. “For the most part, eradication is not a goal in invasive species. When we’re dealing with established species, we’re more likely thinking about ‘how do we reduce the harm?’” said Katie Grzesiak, terrestrial invasive species coordinator for the Michigan Department of Natural Resources. Michigan Invasive Species Program officials recommend prohibiting creeping water-primrose and large flowered water-primrose, since they are not widely distributed in Michigan and difficult to manage. They recommend restricting common butterbur, lesser celandine and round-leaf bittersweet since they are naturalized in Michigan and can be managed to a certain degree. “All those species are high-threat species for which the continued planting in communities likely poses a high financial cost to public agencies in the future and a high cost to nature,” said Matthew Bertrand, Washtenaw County park planner, during public comment at the Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development meeting Tuesday. Related: Michigan restricts buckthorn, other plants as landscapers cry foul Michigan may soon ban sales of this stinky tree and 5 other plants This plant invaded Michigan with ‘chemical warfare.’ Can beetles defeat it? The Michigan Invasive Species Program includes experts from the state’s Department of Agriculture and Rural Development; Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy; and Department of Natural Resources. In selecting the preliminary list, program experts considered how likely the plants are to thrive in Michigan and whether nearby states regulate them. In May, the Michigan Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development put restraints on six invasive species: water hyacinth, water lettuce, common buckthorn, glossy buckthorn, callery pear and Japanese barberry. Many conservation advocates supported the ban, but the Michigan Nursery & Landscape Association opposed regulating them.Donate Officials must complete several steps before any of the latest proposed plants make the prohibited or restricted list. Sign up for our outdoors newsletter Want more coverage like this delivered directly into your inbox? Sign up for the Bridge Michigan Outdoors newsletter here. First, the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development will post the draft order online, likely by the end of Tuesday. A public comment period will then begin on Wednesday and last until Dec. 18. During that time, officials will also present the draft order to the Natural Resources Commission, which can advise but won’t have decisionmaking powers. In January, Michigan Invasive Species Program experts will come before the Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development again and present a summary of public comments. The commission will then have the opportunity to vote on the draft order. Constraints on prohibited plants would begin one month after the order is signed. Regulations on restricted plants would start in January 2029 to allow the plant industry to adjust if businesses sell any of them. Read more about the plants on the list and why the Michigan Invasive Species Program is recommending they be regulated: Common butterbur (Petasites hybridus) Butterbur on a stream in Marquette County (Courtesy of Lake to Lake Cooperative Invasive Species Management Area) Common butterbur is a tall, broad-leafed perennial plant native to Europe and Asia that can clog waterways and is toxic to plant eaters. It is scattered in pockets across Michigan, especially in the Upper Peninsula, but is not commonly sold in the state. The plant is currently regulated in Wisconsin and Minnesota. One recent public commenter requested that it be added to the invasive species list. Lesser celandine (Ficaria verna) Lesser celandine near Cleveland. (Courtesy of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources) Lesser celandine is a small spring ephemeral with yellow flowers that can form dense mats and crowd out native plants. Because it disappears after the spring, it can contribute to erosion. The plant is commonly found in the Grand River watershed in mid-Michigan but is not often sold in the state. It’s currently regulated in a handful of states, including nearby Minnesota, Wisconsin, Illinois and Pennsylvania, and is currently on the invasive species watch list in Michigan. Some recent public commenters requested it be added to the invasive species list. Round-leaf bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus) Round-leaf bittersweet in Brighton State Recreation Area (Courtesy of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources) Roundleaf bittersweet is a leafy, woody, fast-growing vine with red fruit that is sometimes used in holiday decorations. It outcompetes native vines and can interrupt wildlife movement. It is found in most of the state, especially the Lower Peninsula, but is not usually sold here. The plant is currently regulated in about a dozen states, including Wisconsin, Minnesota, Illinois, Indiana and Pennsylvania. A “high” number of recent public commenters requested it be added to the invasive species list. Creeping water-primrose (Ludwigia peploides) Large flowered water-primrose. (Courtesy of Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy) Creeping water-primrose is a floating perennial with yellow flowers that out-competes native species and can form mats in waterways that are difficult to paddle through. It also alters water conditions, reducing oxygen and increasing sedimentation. It is currently sold as a water garden plant in Michigan but has only been spotted in the wild in four counties. That said, the climate in the southern part of the state is a good match for it. It is currently regulated in a few states, including Wisconsin and New York. No recent public commenters requested that it be added to the invasive species list. Large flowered water-primrose (Ludwigia grandiflora) Large flowered water-primrose (Photo via Shutterstock) Large-flowered water-primrose is a floating water plant with large yellow flowers and can be confused with creeping water-primrose. It also forms mats that can out-compete native species and clog waterways, reducing oxygen and increasing sedimentation. It is also currently sold as a water garden plant in Michigan. It may have been spotted in a few counties but genetic identification is needed. Otherwise, it has not yet been found in Michigan. Nearby, it is regulated in a handful of states, including Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and New York nearby. No recent public commenters requested it be added to the invasive species list.

articles.description: Representative-Elect Christina Hines speaks with Stateside's April Baer. Hines will represent Michigan's 10th Congressional District, which includes Macomb County and parts of Oakland County.
articles.content: Democratic 10th Congressional district candidate Christina Hines speaks to supporters on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at her watch party at the UAW Region 1 building in Warren.(Beenish Ahmed / Michigan Public )U.S. Representative-elect Christina Hines beat Republican Mike Bouchard with 52.4% of the vote in Michigan's 10th Congressional District. The district includes Macomb County and parts of Oakland County, and was previously represented by Republican John James. Hines served as an assistant prosecuting attorney in Wayne County before heading up the Special Victims Unit in Washtenaw County. In 2024, she ran for Macomb County Prosecutor, losing to Peter Lucido.Stateside host April Baer spoke with Hines about her path into politics. "You can have systematic change as a line prosecutor, but most of the time, you're helping individuals and you're helping families kind of on a case-by-case basis," Hines said. "And I think that on the legislative side, we have so many opportunities to really change the system."Hines looks forward to supporting a legal system is more victim-centered, she said, and to making sure victim services and law enforcement are fully funded. She also emphasized the need for a bipartisan healthcare policy."When I think about health care, and how bad our system is, it makes me kind of come to this conclusion that I will do anything to try to help fix it..." Hines said. "And I think that it's going to be up to us to find those bipartisan solutions, because I don't want something that only a certain a small percentage of the people here want."Scroll up to hear the full conversation, or read the interview transcript below.Full interview with Christina HinesApril Baer: In your legal life, you were a special victims prosecutor. And I'm wondering what kind of changes you hope to address as representative that you were not able to take on from the courtroom?Christina Hines: Well, you know, I absolutely loved my career. I finished off my career as the chief of the Special Victims Unit and Chief of Appeals. And one thing is that it is hard. You can have systematic change as a line prosecutor, but most of the time you're helping individuals and you're helping families kind of on a case-by-case basis. And I think that on the legislative side, we have so many opportunities to really change the system, right? To make sure that our criminal legal system is more victim-centered, to make sure that we are fully funding law enforcement and our victim services. And I'm really looking forward to tapping into all of those types of things. I mean, I think there's so many opportunities to just protect families, and I'm looking forward to getting started.AB: Christina, you grew up in Macomb County. Can you maybe tell us a little bit about what you see making this region of Michigan and your constituents unique?CH: Well, Macomb County is the best place in the world, if you ask me, having grown up there. You know, Macomb County is nestled like right on Lake St. Clair to our east. This district is about half of the geographical part of Macomb County. So that southern half goes up into Shelby Township. And then we also have the amazing Rochester [and] Rochester Hills in our district too. So there's a lot of things that kind of unite our district, right? We have Selfridge Air National Guard Base and the Detroit Arsenal, as well as a thriving defense and aerospace industry. We have lots of manufacturing with the Big Three and the home of the GM Tech Center. We have bipartisan issues about keeping our our lake and, you know, the Clinton River clean. And so you know, overall, what I will say is that the people in this district work really, really hard to provide for their families, and they want to be able to afford to still live in this community, which has become harder and harder with higher costs. And so I think one of my missions here in Congress is to make sure we are lowering costs so that the people that have built our community can still afford to live in it.AB: Just a couple of years ago, folks would have seen your name on the ballot as you ran for Macomb County Prosecutor, and you were up against an experienced incumbent in that case, Republican Pete Lucido. Did you take any lessons away from that campaign that helped you out in this race?CH: Yeah, I really loved meeting so many people in this coalition. I had never run for any office at that point, but I had volunteered for many other folks as they ran and knocked doors for them. So in that prosecutor's race, you know, I personally knocked on over 7,000 doors. We really hit the ground, and then we kind of expanded that in this congressional race. So my team in this congressional race, just my team alone, hit almost 100,000 doors. And we listened to voters from every single nook and cranny of the district to figure out what their top issues were, so that that was exactly what I'm fighting for. And I take that really seriously here. I think if I were to tell you, you know, my plans moving forward, I know I already said it's costs, but it's also excellent constituent services to make sure that every single individual that calls our office has someone that's going to find exactly what they need, and try to help them through that as quickly and as efficiently and effectively as possible.AB: In addition to affordability and the constituent services piece that you mentioned, one issue that I heard you talk about on the stump was gun reform. I wonder if you're confident that this is still enough of a priority in Congress and among constituents that you and your colleagues could get some meaningful legislation done?CH: One of the jokes that I like to make is that I'm a mom and very, very capable of multitasking. And so we can do all of these things, right? We can focus on lowering costs and on protecting families. One of my big issues that I've talked a lot about is this corruption, right? And these special interests and corporations that are buying off our politicians. When I think about you know, reforms to end gun violence, I think that that corruption is a big part of it. Because overwhelmingly, when I talk to people out in the community, everybody agrees that criminals and people with mental health issues should never be able to get their hands on guns. That young children should never be able to get their hands on guns. These are things that are widely appreciated and supported, and the only reason that we haven't been able to pass that is because of the corruption in D.C. It's the same thing with costs. Until we rein in the corruption, we are never going to be truly able to lower costs. And so I think that we have a lot of missions I've already signed on to a proposal to change the rules to forbid members of the House from trading stocks. I'm going to be working every single day to end the corruption side of things, so that, really, Congress will start delivering for working families.AB: I'm also curious to ask you about the role that you feel immigration reform should play in the next Congress. This is an issue that Donald Trump campaigned on pretty relentlessly. And it appears, from what we learned from voters, that it was one of the issues that lost him some support as ICE's methods ran out of control. You have said that you support increased border security. I believe that all the states on the U.S. southern border flipped blue this cycle. Why would you say this is still a priority in something that's on your mind as you head to Washington?CH: I think that immigration is still on people's minds, even if costs, like I've mentioned, has been top of mind for people. Again, it's one of those things where we can walk and chew gum at the same time. And what happened, I think, was we had a serious issue a couple years ago at the southern border. And then this administration went completely, I mean, overboard, to the point of killing Americans in the street, right? Sending troops into our cities, which is not what people wanted in the first place. There is a difference, I think, in where I'm coming from, of making sure that the people that come into this country come in legally. That we know who they are, and that we know that our communities are safe, right? That is so fair and common sense. And a lot of people want that, versus what has happened under this administration, which is chaos, and going so overboard that American citizens, in addition to so many other non-citizens, are actually getting hurt or killed. And so I think that most people, again, most people that I talk to in our district want common sense immigration reform. And in fact, we have some really amazing immigrant communities in our district: a Ukrainian community, the Chaldean community, the Bengali community ... so many. And I just want to make sure that we have the appropriate bipartisan immigration reform to protect families, to make sure that there's a real, earned pathway to citizenship for people in our district, and also to make sure that we are moving in this country towards common sense approaches to things, instead of the extremes that we have been seeing over the last couple of years.AB: We've been speaking with a number of your colleagues in the newly elected House class, and there are a number of people who've campaigned on a promise of moving forward some health care solutions, including, in some reps' cases, Medicare for All. Is this something you could see yourself getting behind?CH: Well, I think we have a broken health care system right now. I've kind of shared my stories over the years. I'm someone who has been on Medicaid before. I have, you know, helped take care of my mom who had chronic health conditions my entire life, and who passed away. When I think about health care and how bad our system is, it makes me kind of come to this conclusion that I will do anything to try to help fix it. And I think there are a lot of solutions that people have brought forth on the table. And I think that it's going to be up to us to find those bipartisan solutions, because I don't want something that only a certain, small percentage of the people here want. I want something that is bipartisan. And if you look, there are Republicans and Democrats alike and independents in our district that are struggling to pay their healthcare bills, that are struggling to pay their prescriptions. We are seeing, because of the cuts to Medicaid, rural health systems in this country that are going to completely collapse and close. And so we need to have a bipartisan solution in this country that is lasting, and that will help people across the board.AB: What have you heard about the impact within Macomb County? Was was there anything that came to you on the campaign trail about what what the tariffs have meant for for small businesses?CH: Yeah, I mean, I remember talking to a tow truck company owner about how, because of the cost of diesel, he has like 3% margins. And so he was saying, "I've had to increase my prices just in order to stay open, but that makes it harder for individuals to pay." So he's seen a lot of loss of business. He had to cut back on his workforce. And then on the tariff side, I mean, my own husband lost his job as a result of Trump's tariffs over at General Motors. And GM led let go of over 1,200 people as a result of Trump's policies. And so this is all over Macomb and Oakland, right? People all over the Southeast Michigan area are really feeling the impacts every day. And it's not just costs, it's jobs too. So as long as there's no Congress to really check this president, we're going to have problems. So I'm looking forward to January 3rd being part of the solution. Finding ways to lower costs, but also making sure that we're holding this administration accountable.AB: Christina Hines is the representative elect for Michigan's 10th district. She will be starting her new job with the new year. Christina, thank you so much for your time.CH: Thank you, April

articles.description: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. This news analysis was originally distributed in Votebeat’s free weekly newsletter. articles.content: Getty ImagesThis article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. This news analysis was originally distributed in Votebeat’s free weekly newsletter. Sign up to get future editions, including the latest reporting from Votebeat bureaus and curated news from other publications, delivered to your inbox every Saturday. It’s one of the first things you learn if you take high school civics: The national popular vote doesn’t pick the president. The Electoral College does. But there’s a movement afoot to rewrite those lesson plans. And after this month’s elections, its goal — to effectively eliminate the Electoral College — may actually be within reach. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact seeks to solve a simple problem: Sometimes, the winner of the presidential election isn’t the candidate who got the most votes. There have been four times in U.S. history (1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016) when one candidate won the national popular vote but another candidate won the Electoral College — and thus became president. Those elections were followed by calls to abolish the Electoral College — usually from Democrats, who coincidentally were on the losing end of all four. But the Electoral College is written into the Constitution, so ending it would be a very heavy lift. It would require either a constitutional amendment … or a more creative solution like the NPVIC. The proposal is essentially an end run around the Electoral College. States that ratify the compact agree to award their electoral votes not to the winner of that state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. The compact would not take effect until states worth 270 electoral votes (a majority) sign on — but if that happens, their collective action would be enough to guarantee that the national popular vote winner also wins the Electoral College. The compact seemed like a long shot when the organization National Popular Vote first introduced it in 2006. But over the years, more and more states — namely, those controlled by Democrats — have joined. Today, the agreement has 19 signatories worth 222 electoral votes, putting it just 48 shy of taking effect. Those last few votes, though, were always going to be an uphill battle. In order to hit the magic number of 270, the NPVIC needs to pass in several purple states whose leaders have historically been more sympathetic to the Electoral College. But after Democrats’ overwhelming gains in the 2026 election, they will soon hold the reins of power in five such states, worth 61 electoral votes. It’s far from guaranteed that those states will embrace the compact and willingly surrender their outsized influence in presidential elections. (A previous Democratic governor in Nevada vetoed the compact for that very reason.) Moving ahead could very well put a state in the position of awarding its electoral votes to a candidate who failed to win the support of its own voters. But the governor of Pennsylvania and the incoming Senate majority leaders in Arizona and Michigan have expressed openness to joining the compact. If it passes in those three states plus either Wisconsin or Nevada before July 20, 2028, it would be activated in time for that year’s presidential election. Electing the president by popular vote could drastically change the way presidential elections are run. Instead of focusing on just a handful of swing states, campaigns might fan out across the country, giving as much attention to voters in New York and Wyoming as Nevada and Georgia. It might also have major implications for election administration — a close presidential election in one state would no longer require a recount, but a close race nationally could trigger an unprecedented nationwide one. But even if the NPVIC gets to 270 electoral votes, that doesn’t necessarily mean we’ll find out what it’s like to live in a post-Electoral College world. Because that’s when the lawsuits would start flying. “If this does get enough states to put it into force, I think everyone agrees that it will end up in litigation,” said Josh Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky. “And likely this is a good candidate to go up to the Supreme Court.” There are several arguments to be made that the NPVIC is unconstitutional. The most obvious is that it’s too cute by half — that it violates the framers’ intent when they created the Electoral College. While the Constitution gives state legislatures the power to appoint electors however they see fit, some legal scholars argue that historical precedent precludes electors from casting their votes based on election results from outside their states’ borders. Another argument is that the NPVIC violates the compact clause, which says, “No State shall, without the Consent of Congress … enter into any Agreement or Compact with another State.” That’s perhaps not as fatal as it sounds; the Supreme Court in 1893 ruled that congressional signoff is required only for compacts that undermine the supremacy of the federal government. But it’s anyone’s guess whether today’s court would view the NPVIC as doing so. (The NPVIC’s website also says it is “working to obtain support in Congress for the Compact.”) The NPVIC could also violate the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause because it envisions a nationwide election that is conducted under 51 different sets of election laws. Depending on where a voter lives, they may or may not be able to cast a ballot by mail, register to vote at the last minute, or — if they are a convicted felon — even vote at all. But popular vote supporters argue that the amendment simply prohibits states from discriminating against “any person within its jurisdiction.” “I really think this is a close call,” Douglas said about the various cases against the NPVIC. “I think there are good arguments on both sides. I think it’s really hard to predict what the [Supreme] Court will say.” Starting early next year, all eyes will be on Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin to see whether they actually put the compact over the top. If they do, it could set up one of the most closely watched election law cases in history just months before a high-stakes presidential election. Just when it seemed like 2028 couldn’t get more interesting, the NPVIC has gotten our attention. Nathaniel Rakich is Votebeat’s managing editor and is based in Washington, D.C. Contact Nathaniel at nrakich@votebeat.org. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

articles.content: Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives. Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse. [Media: https://www.instagram.com/p/DffPoRdhozI/] Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents. Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness. Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram. Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.
