articles.title: East Lansing’s Sanctuary City Status at Center of Debate Over Federal Grant
articles.description: A $472,000 Department of Justice grant would fund upgrades to city security cameras but includes conditions involving immigration enforcement and DEI programs.
articles.content: East Lansing could soon accept a large federal grant to upgrade its security cameras, but the grant appears to come with conditions that conflict with East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and diversity, equity and inclusion programming. The city has been awarded and could accept a $472,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Justice, or DOJ, that pays for upgrades for up to 350 security cameras. The city’s cameras are a decade old and the new cameras will have better image quality and motion detection, according to the staff report. However, the grant comes with a series of conditions. One condition states recipients “may not prohibit, or in any way restrict, any government entity or official from sending to, receiving from, maintaining, or exchanging information regarding citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, of any individual with components of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or any other federal, state or local government entity.” Another condition says that by accepting the grant, recipients certify they do not operate diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The grant also stipulates recipients must comply with all presidential memoranda and executive orders. The East Lansing City Council could accept the grant funding by approving the consent agenda at its meeting Tuesday night, a possibility that has some residents concerned about East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and other stances. East Lansing officials say accepting the grant would not force any policy changes and the city is asking the DOJ to remove the conditions. East Lansing’s mayor said if the federal government tries to challenge or revoke the funding, the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed. Residents are concerned that accepting the grant contradicts the city’s current sanctuary city status. The resolution declaring East Lansing a sanctuary city states that in a manner consistent with state and federal law, city officials will not actively collaborate with federal agents solely for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration law. Further, East Lansing employs a DEI director. “I have grave concerns that by accepting this grant money, that the city is committing to cooperating with the U.S. Department of Justice when it comes to immigration enforcement,” said Karen Hoene, chair of the city’s Human Rights Commission. “This is very concerning considering the fact that we are a sanctuary city and we have City Council members that have committed to remaining a sanctuary city.” Hoene said that the City Council placing the resolution to accept the grant funding on the consent agenda, which is usually passed without discussion, is “sneaky” and feels like a “MAGA move.” But city officials say the grant does not force it to change any of its operations. Councilmember Mark Meadows said the city’s policy is that officials do not communicate with federal officials on immigration enforcement, except in cases where federal law requires it. He said this will continue to be how the city operates. Meadows said conditions the grant places are illegal and courts have ruled cities don’t have to comply with these regulations. He said the federal government cannot force municipalities to assist in federal immigration enforcement. “It’s just another example of Trump’s administration trying to, I guess, create law that doesn’t exist,” Meadows said. “That’s how we’ve approached it. “If they want to yank the grant, then they’ll have the opportunity to yank the grant. But we haven’t changed anything,” he continued. “We’re accepting it. If we get the money, they can order us to return the money. We’ll deal with that at that point in time.” Mayor Erik Altmann said in a call on Tuesday that the city believes the conditions are unenforceable due to injunctions and court rulings. He pointed to a two-page memorandum that was added to the City Council agenda at some point on Tuesday after residents had reached out to East Lansing Info about the grant conditions. The memorandum from Interim City Manager Annette Irwin, dated Nov. 18 – which is tomorrow – asks that the conditions referencing DEI, immigration enforcement and executive orders be removed. The memo argues that the conditions are not enforceable. Altmann said accepting the grant does not change the city’s policies and the plan is to continue operating in the same way. He said he does not know how the federal government will respond. “The problem is that we are in completely uncharted territory here,” Altmann said. “I have no idea because nobody can predict what the Trump administration is going to do on a given day.” If the federal government does seek to challenge or revoke the funding, Altmann said the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed. “That is a conversation we will have to have, not just at the council level but at the community level if we get to that point,” he said. “We have a bunch of people writing to us at the City Council account saying basically ‘don’t take a half-million-dollar grant,’” Altmann continued. “There’s probably a lot of other people in the community who say ‘You better take a half-million-dollar grant.’” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on […]
articles.content: Voters mark their ballots on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Alaska, Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Senate took a first step Tuesday toward reviving the moribund Federal Election Commission, holding a confirmation hearing on President Donald Trump’s nominees to lead the campaign finance watchdog after it was sidelined for the midterm elections. The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on complaints or issuing advisory opinions. As its backlog of work has grown, candidates and political groups have been left uncertain about when — or if — the FEC will take action on alleged violations of federal campaign finance law. The Senate Rules and Administration Committee on Tuesday weighed the nominations of two Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson, to join the FEC. Only two commissioners, both Democrats, are currently serving and the agency needs a bipartisan quorum of at least four to take official action. “Restoring the commission’s ability to function is especially important following the 2026 midterm elections,” said Sen. Bill Hagerty, a Tennessee Republican who chaired the hearing. Hagerty pointed to the backlog of complaints and the need to prepare for the 2028 presidential race. Restoring a quorum will allow the FEC “to resume its essential responsibilities,” he said. The FEC enforces federal campaign finance laws and assists candidates and donors in complying with them. The FEC, which marked its 50th anniversary in 2025, also makes public a vast trove of campaign finance data. The hearing marked an effort by Republicans to end the FEC’s dormancy during the Senate’s lame-duck period before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. At that point, Democrats will have much more power to demand that the White House nominate individuals acceptable to Democrats or block Trump’s nominees. Democrats support restoring a quorum on the FEC, but they question whether Trump will allow commissioners to act independently. In February 2025, Trump fired the Democratic chair of the FEC, Ellen Weintraub, who had been a commissioner since 2002. Weintraub has said she doesn’t view the firing as legally valid, though she hasn’t challenged the dismissal in court. The move against Weintraub came after Republican Sean Cooksey resigned before Trump’s inauguration. In April 2025, Republican Allen Dickerson also resigned, creating a lack of a quorum that has persisted. Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said Tuesday the FEC was established in the post-Watergate era to be evenly balanced between Democrats and Republicans and politically independent. Padilla is the ranking Democrat on the committee but will likely chair the panel beginning in January. “It’s absolutely critical that any commissioners who sign on to help lead this agency commit to restoring and defending that independence. Full stop,” Padilla said. The Trump administration has broadly sought to bring independent agencies created by Congress under the control of the White House. The U.S. Supreme Court in June allowed the president to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission without cause. It’s not clear how that decision would apply to firings of members of the FEC. Pledges of neutrality Stow and Woodson promised to act impartially and emphasized the importance of the bipartisan nature of the FEC. But they evaded questions about how they would specifically act toward Trump’s political operation, MAGA, Inc. because complaints about the super PAC could come before the commission. “Should I be confirmed, I pledge to discharge my duties with impartiality and unwavering commitment to the First Amendment and enforcement of the law as enacted by Congress and interpreted by the nation’s courts,” said Stow, a longtime FEC lawyer from Texas. Woodson, a Virginia lawyer focused on campaign finance at the law firm Wiley Rein LLP, worked at the FEC from 2013 to 2015. He said the FEC must always act with sensitivity for First Amendment rights, and that its guidance and regulations should “promote freedom, not frustration.” “Everyone that will come before me, I will treat exactly the same — impartially,” Woodson said, whether they hold “the highest office in the land” or are “just an ordinary congressperson.” Trump nominated Stow and Woodson in February, but Tuesday’s hearing marked the Senate’s first public step toward advancing their nominations. Push for quorum On Nov. 5, a dozen former Republican FEC commissioners wrote to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, asking that he prioritize their confirmations before the end of the current Congress. The FEC’s situation is “increasingly untenable,” the former commissioners wrote. In addition to being unable to take action on complaints and issue guidance about campaign finance law, the group noted that hackers had targeted the FEC, crippling its online system for reporting campaign finance information in the closing days of the midterm elections. The former commissioners wrote that the incident offered a “stark reminder” that the FEC is responsible for maintaining critical systems that allow the American public to receive campaign finance information. “An agency carrying responsibilities of that magnitude should have a functioning Commission at its head,” the group wrote.

articles.title: FDA Launches the Global Reliance Disclosure Program to Expand Patient Access to Medicines Worldwide
articles.description: FDA today announced the Global Reliance Disclosure Program (GRDP), a landmark initiative that will fundamentally transform how the FDA's regulatory drug and biologic approval decisions are leveraged by health authorities around the world.
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced the Global Reliance Disclosure Program (GRDP), a landmark initiative that will fundamentally transform how the FDA's regulatory drug and biologic approval decisions are leveraged by health authorities around the world. The GRDP marks a major step forward in the FDA's global leadership and may accelerate patient access to innovative therapies throughout the world. The GRDP enables the FDA to more efficiently share minimally redacted approval packages, including the FDA's detailed scientific and regulatory assessments, directly with companies who can then share them with regulatory authorities outside of the United States, empowering those authorities to rely on the FDA's rigorous, science-based review decisions rather than conducting duplicative and time-consuming product evaluations of their own, while maintaining sovereignty over their regulatory decision. "The GRDP is a prime example of America First policies improving public health worldwide," said Grace Graham, FDA Deputy Commissioner for Policy, Legislation, and International Affairs. "The FDA is the global gold standard and making it easier for applicants to leverage our detailed scientific assessments to facilitate faster access for patients everywhere is an example of America’s continued interest in advancing global health under the Trump Administration." The GRDP launched on Oct. 30, with a President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) tentative approval for lenacapavir, a drug indicated for both HIV prevention and treatment. This is an especially meaningful starting point given PEPFAR's life-saving mission to combat HIV/AIDS in some of the world's most vulnerable populations. The GRDP is currently available to PEPFAR tentative approvals, excluding tentatively approved abbreviated new drug application products. However, the FDA intends to expand the GRDP in January 2027 to all novel drug and biologics (New Molecular Entity New Drug Applications and 351(a) Biologics License Applications), dramatically broadening the program's reach and impact. The FDA also intends to launch a pathway in early 2027 to expedite an applicant’s ability to request their minimally redacted action packages for approved and licensed drugs and biologics, accelerating global access to medicines that are already on the market in the United States and have been found to be safe and effective by the FDA. To receive a minimally redacted application approval package as part of the GRDP, applicants must request to participate within 10 calendar days of approval and confirm the application package is being submitted to a foreign regulatory authority in support of a marketing application. Applicants with eligible GRDP applications will receive detailed information in FDA approval letters and the agency intends to provide the minimally redacted package on an expedited basis. Requests for minimally redacted approval packages for other purposes will not be processed under the GRDP and should be submitted as a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. “In an era of increasing global interdependence in pharmaceutical development and supply chains, the FDA's leadership is most effective when it is collaborative,” said Mark Abdoo, FDA Associate Commissioner for Global Policy and Strategy. “The GRDP reflects a forward-looking vision of regulatory leadership: one defined not by exclusivity, but by the willingness to share expertise, elevate global standards, and put patients first — wherever they are.” The GRDP addresses one of the most persistent and consequential challenges in global health: the gap between regulatory approval in high-capacity countries and patient access in lower-resource settings. When a drug is approved by the FDA, patients in many parts of the world may wait months or years longer for their own national health authority to complete an independent review due to limited regulatory capacity and resources. Beyond individual product approvals, the GRDP supports global health security. Harmonized regulatory decisions reduce the risk of fragmented or inconsistent product standards across markets, helping to ensure that the same high-quality therapies reach patients regardless of where they live, including here in the United States. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

articles.title: Opinion | Michigan has delayed water upgrades long enough. Lansing needs to act
articles.description: A new report says upgrading Michigan’s aging water and sewer infrastructure will cost $85 billion over 20 years. Residents cannot pay it alone in rates.
articles.content: I grew up in Michigan when the water worked. I never thought about where it came from or if it would stop. In Akron, a village in the Thumb, people don’t have that luxury. Fighting a house fire can leave residents unable to drink their water. An estimated 98% of the system dates to its 1950s construction. Only 2 of 5 wells are usable. Draw enough water to fight a structure fire and the water system pressures can drop far enough to trigger a boil-water advisory. Suzanne R. Coffey is chief executive officer of the Great Lakes Water Authority, which serves nearly 4 million customers in Michigan. (Courtesy photo) Akron is not an outlier. It is part of the pattern. The Water Funding Task Force, convened by the Great Lakes Water Authority, spent six months examining Michigan’s more than 1,400 community water systems and hearing similar accounts from every region: infrastructure is aging faster than local revenue can replace it. The ensuing report, “The Crisis Beneath Us,” put the price of catching up as high as $85 billion over the next 20 years. When a 54-inch transmission main broke in southwest Detroit in February 2025, it flooded a square mile of a densely populated neighborhood in the middle of winter. Hundreds of people were forced to leave their homes, some for weeks. When a main failed in Oakland County in May and cut service to roughly 200,000 people, schools closed, a company sent its headquarters home and nursing home residents were moved out of their community. Only about a third of the total cost for system disruptions like these fall on the utility that owns the pipe. The other two-thirds lands on everyone else: the restaurant closed on its busiest day, the hospital rescheduling procedures, the employee who loses a shift. In Grand Traverse County this August, a failed sewer line sent sewage up through South Airport Road, closed it indefinitely and put Boardman Lake and the Boardman River under a no-contact advisory in the middle of the busy tourist season. A community pays for a main break whether or not it owns the water main. The infrastructure itself is where the arithmetic is unforgiving. Many Michigan cities built the bulk of their systems during two bursts of growth, in the 1920s and the years after World War II, and designed them to last 75 to 100 years. Currently, less than 1& of Michigan’s water mains are replaced in any given year and most are already more than 50 years old. Michigan spent the first half of the 20th century building this infrastructure and the second half asking local communities to maintain it alone. Federal support, which once covered a substantial share of water infrastructure spending nationally, has receded to a fraction of that, and the state never replaced it. We built dedicated, sustained funding for roads and bridges and never built the equivalent for water. Today, for every dollar Michigan spends on roads, water infrastructure receives only about four cents.Donate Local rates were never designed to carry the difference. They were meant to keep systems going – to cover treatment, staffing, chemicals and repairs, not wholesale replacement of a system assembled over a century. Combined water and sewer rates across Michigan have risen 24 percent in five years, and the gap continues to grow. There is no rate structure that could ever close it. Other states have confronted this and acted. The task force’s research examined utilities in Wisconsin, Illinois and Ohio that have built predictable, multi-year funding structures that supplement rates and charges. Last November, voters in Texas amended their state constitution to dedicate ongoing revenue to water infrastructure, and they did it overwhelmingly. Michigan has not had that conversation, and now there are complex choices ahead about how a sustained state commitment gets funded. Those choices belong to the Legislature and ultimately to voters. For most of my life, this system was invisible because it was working. That same level of service, a working system, is what we owe our children and grandchildren and those who come after them, and we are not currently on course to deliver it. As the largest water and sewer system in the state, GLWA serves more than 100 communities across southeast Michigan. This gives us a view across systems that any single utility simply doesn’t have. It comes with an obligation to use that vantage point on behalf of communities facing the same pressures with fewer resources. We cannot solve this alone. No utility can, whatever its size. What we can do is make sure the problem is visible, measured and understood, and then help build a coalition capable of acting on it. Not two days after the Crisis Beneath Us was released, we convened the first of many coalition building meetings to hear from municipal leagues, townships, counties, contractors and business organizations. Those who sat down with us as part of this initial meeting did not need persuading. Neither, I suspect, does most of Michigan. What we need now from Lansing is a plan – a sustained, multiyear commitment to water infrastructure – and the political will to fund it.

What is kratom? Michigan physicians warn of addiction and health risks
articles.description: Michigan family physicians are warning against the effects of kratom, an herbal drug from Southeast Asia which has found a large market in the United States.
articles.content: Kratom leaves.(Bigc Studio - stock.adobe.com / 522161772)Michigan family physicians are warning against the effects of kratom, an herbal drug from Southeast Asia that has found an increasingly large market in the United States.In low doses, kratom acts as a stimulant. At higher doses, it becomes a sedative. Over the past year, it has been subject to increasing calls for regulations at the federal and state level.Dr. Eliza Hutchinson, director of addiction services at Packard Health, discussed the drug in a panel Tuesday with other members of the Michigan Academy of Family Physicians.“I'm often asked, 'Is kratom good or is kratom bad?'” Hutchinson said. “And I think we all want a simple answer to that question, but the reality really is more complex.”What is kratom?Kratom comes in two main forms. Natural leaf kratom has existed for hundreds of years and is a comparatively mild drug. Concentrated kratom products such as 7-OH and other synthetic alternatives are newer. They are far more potent and have much more severe side effects.Hutchinson said she has seen some patients responsibly use natural leaf kratom for chronic pain relief. People who use products such as 7-OH and other highly potent alternatives are much more likely to experience addiction and other negative symptoms.“These products are often marketed as safe and natural, and in reality, they can also be harmful," Hutchinson said. “We see them causing problems such as seizures, liver failure, overdose, or often in my practice, addiction.” DEA photo of leave of kratom tree and kratom capsules(Department of Justice/Drug Enforcement Agency)Can you die from kratom use?While it is not common, some people have died from kratom-related overdoses. While traditional botanical leaf kratom remains unregulated at a federal level, some synthetic kratom products were recently recategorized as Schedule I drugs, which means they have high potential for abuse and face severe federal restrictions on their production and distribution.Kratom, even in its natural leaf form, has not been approved by the Federal Drug Administration for medical or any other use. Individuals considering using the drug medicinally in any capacity are advised to first consult with a licensed healthcare professional.The drug’s use has increased significantly in recent years. A study by the University of Michigan and Texas State University found that more than 5 million Americans have tried kratom. The majority of people who previously or currently used kratom also had substance use disorders associated with it or another drug.“Where I work, kratom usage has impacted many individuals and families,” said Jennifer Morse, director of the central and mid-Michigan district health departments. “The stories of deaths are devastating, and the addiction can be very challenging to understand.”Is kratom legal in Michigan?Kratom is not currently regulated in Michigan, and any products not banned at a federal level may be bought at smoke shops or even gas stations across the state. That may soon change, however.Michigan’s state House of Representatives passed a bill that would ban growing, synthesizing or selling the drug in the state, though it has not yet been considered by the state Senate.Anyone struggling with kratom addiction can seek help with their healthcare providers or dial the National 988 Crisis Lifeline.

articles.title: FDA Approves First Drug Shown to Help Patients with Infantile-Onset Niemann-Pick Disease Type C Live Longer
articles.description: FDA approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) injection, the first treatment shown to help people with a severe form of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) live longer.
articles.content: New therapy offers a meaningful treatment option for families facing a rare and serious childhood disease The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) injection, the first treatment shown to help people with a severe form of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) live longer. Lembaz is approved to reduce the risk of death in adult and pediatric patients who weigh at least 7 kg (about 15 pounds) and whose neurological symptoms began before age 6, also known as infantile-onset NPC. “For families living with Niemann-Pick disease type C, today’s approval marks an important milestone,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “For the first time, there is a treatment shown to help adults and children with this serious disease live longer, and we are committed to continuing to support the development of therapies for the rare disease community.” Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder affecting an estimated 1 in 150,000 people, in which the body cannot properly process cholesterol and other fats inside cells. Over time, these substances accumulate — particularly in the brain — causing progressive neurological decline, including loss of movement, coordination, and the ability to swallow. Patients whose neurological symptoms begin before age 6 face the most serious form of the disease. Prior to this approval action, two therapies were approved for NPC, but neither has been shown to reduce the risk of death. Both carry age and weight restrictions that limit access for the youngest and most seriously affected patients. Lembaz is the first FDA-approved therapy to reduce the risk of death in adults and children weighing at least 7 kg (about 15 pounds) with NPC whose neurological symptoms began before age 6. A trained healthcare provider gives Lembaz as an injection directly into the spinal canal — a procedure called an intrathecal injection — every two weeks. To assess whether Lembaz reduced the risk of death, the FDA examined the survival of 36 patients treated with Lembaz across three clinical studies and an expanded access program. All patients had neurological manifestations of NPC that occurred prior to age 6. Patients treated with Lembaz had longer overall survival compared to the matched external control group, with a 55% reduction in the risk of death. The median survival time was 8.5 years for the treated group compared with 4.9 years in the control group. This survival benefit was observed regardless of whether patients were also taking miglustat, a therapy used off-label in NPC. The most common side effects of Lembaz include problems with hearing, balance and coordination, fatigue, vomiting, back pain, headache, fever, diarrhea, nausea, and cough. Lembaz carries a boxed warning for hearing impairment, including permanent hearing loss. A comprehensive hearing evaluation should be performed on patients before starting Lembaz and regularly throughout treatment, and dose adjustments may be needed based on the results of these evaluations. Lembaz received Breakthrough Therapy designation. The FDA granted approval of Lembaz to Mandos, LLC, a subsidiary of Beren Therapeutics, PBC. articles.content: Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need. Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or texting it. [Video: Tasks in Gemini texting] Google first introduced its Spark AI agent in May, but it was only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The launch of tasks in Gemini brings Spark’s capabilities to all users in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia, and India. You can find tasks by opening Gemini and changing the toggle on the homepage from “Chat” to “Tasks.” [Video: Google Gemini Tasks] Tasks in Gemini is just one of the many agentic AI features that have emerged over the past year, including Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots, and Meta’s Muse. Google says Gemini will perform tasks in a “hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users.” You can also provide instructions for Gemini while it completes tasks. When performing more sensitive tasks, like purchasing an item, it will stop working and ask for your permission before following through.

articles.title: Detroit delays vote on $2.2-billion RenCen project as public comments pour in
articles.description: Bedrock and General Motors hope the vote will be finalized before Thanksgiving, but council members say they need more time to review their request for $548 million in tax subsidies.
articles.content: GM's Headquarters in Detroit(John F. Martin / Creative Commons / http://j.mp/1SPGCl0)The Detroit City Council delayed its vote today on a $2.2 billion project that would demolish two towers of the Renaissance Center to make way for new housing and a riverfront park. The decision to move forward with the project, originally expected during today’s meeting, is pushed back to next week's meeting, which will be the council's last formal session of the year.While developers Bedrock and General Motors aimed to have the vote finalized before Thanksgiving, council members say they need more time to review their request for $548 million in tax subsidies, an ask many Detroiters say is too high. That’s despite developers pledging a $133-million community benefits package in exchange. Community members and advocacy groups view the allocation of massive public funds to private developers as a misuse of the city's wealth.Theo Pride, an organizer with the Detroit People’s Platform who joined a protest against the project last week, condemned the proposed subsidies as a "land grab" by the state's wealthiest interests."That's a half a billion dollars of our public wealth that should be going to our babies, that should be going to our seniors," Pride said. "Yet it's going to someone worth more, actually double than the yearly income of every single Detroiter combined."More than 130 community members and advocates signed up to share their opinions during a public comment period that stretched for hours. Some residents argued the approval process is too rushed and lacks transparency, while others believe the renovations are exactly what the city needs to boost its overall appeal.Pastor Spencer Ellis spoke in support of the project, sharing a conversation he had with his son who moved to Chicago after graduation.“He already called and said, ‘Dad, I'm not ever coming back to Detroit,'” Ellis recalled. “Not because he doesn’t love Detroit, but because there’s not a lot of entertainment, not a lot of things to do in Detroit for our young people.”A 3D conceptual site plan illustrating the proposed "East Riverfront Concept Plan."(Bedrock)“There’s nothing wrong with development, but don’t push us out,” said Rev. Sharon Buttry with the Detroit Hamtramck Coalition for Advancing Healthy Environments. She pushed the council for more transparency: “We need you to support us and advocate for us that’s why we elected you."Small business owners and Wayne State University students said they were encouraged by the jobs, skills training, and economic boost the project would have.“This is a generational impact that will have an impact across the city, but also trickle down to Southwest Detroit. And I know that our beloved council member (Gabriela) Santiago-Romero will make sure that the jobs follow,” said Mary Carmen Muñoz, director of Latin Americans for Social and Economic Development, Inc.If the council ultimately approves the package next week, the massive redevelopment will roll out in three phases with a projected completion date in 2038.

articles.title: Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
articles.description: Introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, with better professional outputs, coding, computer use, and efficiency at lower cost across ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API.
articles.content: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design. On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost. Agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model. We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works. In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task. Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks. In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max). FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging. Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released LifeVal evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost. LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis. We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler. Harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. Astra for Law, our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark. Harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations. Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of GDPval that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol. GDPval v2 consists of long-horizon knowledge-work assignments from real projects in sectors like finance, data science, biotechnology, and marketing. Building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts. GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into new slides. Early testers found the decks easier to use directly with fewer edits, thanks to titles that state the main takeaway and concise body copy that focuses on the details readers need. We evaluated GPT-6.2 Astra on turning dense information into readable briefs and infographics for both technical and non-technical audiences. Examples included trading briefs and diagrams of agentic workflows. GPT-6.2 Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. The writing and charts made it much easier to pick out the key points of a briefing, and the diagrams clarified complex systems by showing how the parts work together. In our Agent evals, GPT-6.2 Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks. Astra was strongest on legal research, scoring higher than alternative models on 8 of the 10 research tasks we tested, across tax, M&A and litigation work. GPT-6.2 Astra is a notable step up from GPT-6 Astra, completing more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks in our evaluations with 34.5% fewer output tokens. For internal memos drafting tasks, GPT-6.2 Astra caught more weaknesses in the client’s position, and drafted filings made fewer unwarranted concessions. On the apps, dashboards and slides ClickUp Brain builds inside the workspace, GPT-6.2 Astra edged out our production model in blind testing. What stood out was how it got there: about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds. GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype. We asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to quickly test new designs and improve simulation accuracy over time. GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior. Our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp. GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site. Those gains in visual reasoning and computer use carry over to 3D design. GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, from a pinball table you can play to a recreation of the Colosseum you can explore from different angles. On Artificial Analysis’s AA‑3D, human judges try two blinded experiences built from the same prompt and vote for the one they prefer. GPT‑6.2 Astra ranks first with 1,318 Elo, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT‑6.2 Sol at 1,259. GPT-6.2 Astra is a huge leap forward for creative work. It makes Higgsfield Miracle possible, powering real-time video editing with pixel-level precision and giving creators ultimate creative control. In our internal 3D generation evals, it achieved the target result in one shot in 73% of cases, while GPT-6 Astra needed three or more iterations. This saves our creative team a lot of time and allows for more efficient fully agentic workflows. GPT‑6.2 Astra has better judgment about how to execute a task, including matching its tools and effort to the workflow, and knowing when to use plugins versus computer use. On coding, GPT-6.2 Astra is better at implementing and testing complex changes in existing codebases. Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision. GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like GPT‑6 Astra, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework. Due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through OpenAI Daybreak, defenders can currently access GPT‑6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, in addition to our alpha for GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑6 Cyber for advanced, authorized security testing on Daybreak Red. We will work to bring GPT‑6.2 models to Daybreak. We highlight key benchmark results below, using internal testing configurations with cybersecurity safeguards and classifiers disabled. See the accompanying system card(opens in a new window) for full results and methodology. Developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. PHP2Shell(opens in a new window) showed how AI can help researchers uncover critical flaws. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior. We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to monitor models and intervene when needed. Like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our Preparedness Framework. Scholten, Michigan Head Start Association criticize Trump rollback of teacher pay increases
articles.description: A new federal rule rolled back an expected $10,000 pay raise for most Head Start program teachers, as well as basic benefits for full-time staff — a move that has met pushback in Michigan from an association of teachers and U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids). The rule, promulgated by the U.S. The Department of […]
articles.content: Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)A new federal rule rolled back an expected $10,000 pay raise for most Head Start program teachers, as well as basic benefits for full-time staff — a move that has met pushback in Michigan from an association of teachers and U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids). The rule, promulgated by the U.S. The Department of Health and Human Services under President Donald Trump, was finalized over the weekend. Issued in May, the “Restoring Flexibility to Support Head Start Program Access” rule cancels the mandatory pay increase for Head Start teachers and expanded benefits set forward in 2024 by the administration of former President Joe Biden. Head Start leaders had requested an overall 4.97% cost-of-living adjustment, often referred to as COLA, which would have allowed programs to pay staff at a more competitive rate. That increase also had the potential to retain experienced educators while allowing families to continue receiving consistent Head Start services. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Health and Human Services rule rescinded requirements put forward by the Biden administration to provide full-time staff with health care coverage, paid leave and behavioral health access. Part-time staff were also eligible for healthcare access and other benefits. Although it is separate from an August Health and Human Services proposed rewrite of Head Start performance standards, concern remains for Head Start teachers now cut out from receiving higher pay and benefits. The Biden rule would have affected more than 250,000 teachers and staff, and the Trump course change may put nearly 716,000 children and their families’ education access at risk. “Programs will no longer be required to move toward pay comparable to public preschool teachers by 2031, leaving currently low wages stagnant for Head Start educators and encouraging qualified and valued individuals to seek other employment opportunities outside of our programs,” the Michigan Head Start Association said in a social media post. “Our educators are the heart of our classrooms and the foundation of Head Start’s success. Without the professional and supportive education they provide, fewer children and families can be served in Head Start programs. Families will lose access to critical early learning and interventions because of insufficient operational and financial federal investment.” Scholten also criticized the new rule, noting that she joined a June letter opposing the decision. “The Trump Administration’s decision to cancel cost-of-living adjustments for Head Start teachers sends a clear message about its priorities: penny-pinching educators’ salaries while covering the White House in gold. This is unacceptable,” Scholten said in a statement. “For more than 60 years, Head Start has supported early education, health and dental care, and healthy meals while connecting families to job training and housing support. Now, the program is asking for the bare minimum: funding to maintain its operations and to help absorb higher costs amid the affordability crisis.” Scholten added that the decision would force Head Start programs to “choose between a livable wage for educators, spaces for more children, and healthy meals on the table.” “I have heard directly from my constituents who run these programs about how this will negatively impact our community,” Scholten said. “This is unacceptable, and I will keep fighting to protect Head Start, because the educators and families who depend on it deserve better than this.”

articles.content: A track in which half of R.E.M. ends up in the studio. It’s very easy to fall in love with Stef Chura. She’s got charisma and swagger on stage. There’s conviction in her voice, too. articles.content: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. articles.content: Swarms of buzzing Ukrainian drones have filled the skies from the Black Sea to Moscow in recent nights in an unrelenting aerial blitz that poses a serious test of Russia’s defenses. A record high number of Ukrainian drones shot down by the military overnight Monday was topped 24 hours later, when it reported downing 1,441 of them, the most brought down since the start of the full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Among the targets hit was a landmark bridge to Crimea that was seriously damaged in a blow to Moscow’s pride. The Russian military, in turn, ramped up its missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to disrupt electricity and heat as winter sets in. Two key bridges in Kyiv were seriously damaged by Moscow’s attacks. AP correspondent Charles de Ledesma reports Ukraine has struck a major Russian bridge with drones and missiles, as aerial attacks escalate. The surge in aerial attacks follows a week that saw little progress in the first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months. Here’s a look at Russia’s air defenses as it fends off challenges posed by Ukraine’s attacks: Russia has more land than any other country in the world, and protecting that vast space is a major challenge despite its massive arsenal of defensive systems. “Russia’s air defense system, like many air defense systems around the world, is not necessarily designed to protect the entirety of Russia’s territory and the air approaches to the country,” said Thomas Withington, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute. While Ukrainian drones cruise at about 150 kph (about 95 mph), they fly very low, making it harder for radar to spot them. Their range allows them to strike deep inside Russia. In one recent attack, they hit an oil refinery in Omsk in eastern Siberia, about 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) from the border. While their payload of about 50 kilograms (110 pounds) is relatively small, their precision allows them to inflict massive damage to such facilities and other infrastructure. Ukraine also has used long-range Flamingo cruise missiles, capable of reaching up to 950 kph (590 mph), carrying a much heavier payload. Kyiv has fewer of these missiles than drones. Like in previous attacks, the number of Ukrainian drones reported downed by Russia early Monday couldn’t be independently verified, and official reports haven’t said how many actually got through air defenses to hit their targets. Withington noted that as a general rule of thumb, 10% get through and hit their targets. “It’s a game of averages,” he said, so launching more drones means that more get through. He said Russia’s air defenses, like most integrated air-defense systems around the world, are designed to shoot down aircraft, air launched weapons and ballistic missiles, and thus could struggle to engage drones. “Drones are a very different calculus, and because of it, the performance of those systems is never going to be as optimal as it would be against a conventional threat,” he said, adding that while air defenses shoot down or jam most of them, some will always get through. While Russian air defenses around key facilities such as refineries have been bolstered, Ukrainian drones have continued to set them ablaze. The large size of the targets makes them more vulnerable, Withington said, adding that Ukraine has learned a lot about the operation of Russia’s air defense systems, enabling the military to polish its tactics and find loopholes. “All of Russia’s air defenses, all of the systems they deployed, by and large have given up their secrets” after years of fighting, he said. “The more of that information and data you are armed with, the easier it becomes to defeat Russian air defenses.” In June, a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and also hit a nearby naval base, casting a cloud over President Vladimir Putin’s showcase economic forum in his hometown. Putin acknowledged the damage from the attacks, saying Russia would strengthen its air defenses. Over the past two nights, Ukraine used missiles and drones to hit the Kerch Bridge that links the mainland and the Crimean Peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. One section of the bridge collapsed Tuesday, halting vehicular traffic. “Unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100% protection for various facilities against such massive strikes,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. From the early stages of the conflict, Russian authorities have prioritized protecting Moscow. Media reports said additional air defense systems have been put on the outskirts of the capital, and some could be seen on top of some of the Moscow buildings, including the Defense Ministry’s headquarters facing the Gorky Park across the Moskva River. While Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin repeatedly claimed that the bulk of the drones were downed, it’s impossible to independently verify his claims. Despite the dense protection around the capital, Ukrainian drones have managed to pierce the shield. Russia scaled down the annual May 9 Victory Day parade, fearing Ukrainian drone strikes. Days later, a massive drone attack on Moscow’s suburbs killed three people. Successive attacks repeatedly struck the oil refinery on the outskirts of the capital, disrupting its operation. Another top priority has been to protect Putin’s residence in Valdai in northwestern Russia. In December 2025, Russian authorities reported a massive Ukrainian attack on the residence but claimed that none of the 91 drones hit the target. Since Soviet times, Russia has developed a broad array of air defense systems, from portable ones to long-range weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles. The S-400 Triumph is the main long-range air defense system capable of spotting and engaging aircraft and ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 400 kilometers (about 250 miles). The even more potent S-500 Prometheus system that reaches as far as 600 kilometers (about 370 miles) also is available in small numbers. Russia also uses various models of S-300 air defense missile systems, an older but still very advanced and powerful long-range weapon. For shorter ranges, the military has relied on the Pantsyr, the Tor and the Buk air defense systems. While Buk and Tor use missiles to shoot down aerial targets, Pantsyr can use a combination of guns and missiles. A Pantsyr system sits atop the Defense Ministry building in Moscow. Russia also has deployed teams armed with shoulder-fired Igla and Verba air defense missiles and machine guns for protection of key facilities. Helicopter gunships also are involved. Withington said Ukraine and Russia could be expected to further ramp up the number of attacking drones to overwhelm air defenses. “The long-term direction of travel, both for Ukraine and Russia, will be a continued exponential increase in the number of drones that can be launched at any given time,” he said.

articles.title: House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks
articles.description: A new House majority can push climate policy, but a full US return remains uncertain.
articles.content: A new House majority can push climate policy, but a full US return remains uncertain. ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy. “The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said. President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs. Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities. Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks. Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities. “The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News. The US would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman said. “We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.). The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.). Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts. “We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.). “I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added. It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said. “But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.” Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena. “We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.” Singh said the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power. “As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.” Singh said until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.” Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress. “What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added. While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks. “The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.” Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies. This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

articles.title: Experts credit smooth midterms to election workers, Democratic rout
articles.description: After President Donald Trump’s aggressive push for control over elections, this month’s midterms went smoothly because of the resilience of state and local officials and Democrats’ sweeping victories, several election experts said Monday. Nearly two weeks after Election Day, a panel of researchers and former local government officials expressed relief that the election system held. […]
articles.content: An election worker feeds ballots into a verification and sorting machine at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)After President Donald Trump’s aggressive push for control over elections, this month’s midterms went smoothly because of the resilience of state and local officials and Democrats’ sweeping victories, several election experts said Monday. Nearly two weeks after Election Day, a panel of researchers and former local government officials expressed relief that the election system held. But panelists at the discussion, hosted virtually by the Safeguarding Democracy Project at the University of California, Los Angeles, also warned against complacency about future contests. “It didn’t happen magically,” said Bill Gates, executive director of Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory, which supports efforts to combat election misinformation. Election officials and voting rights advocates had braced for a chaotic aftermath to the election, including potential federal interference in voting. Election workers across the country gameplanned how they would react if federal agents showed up at the polls or tried to disrupt vote counting. But on Election Day, no major incidents occurred and voting proceeded without federal interference. Gates and others credited election workers, saying their preparation — including for the possibility of disruption — ultimately helped ensure smooth voting. “They were really concerned about federal intervention. It was their top concern at every single one of our events in the last year,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at Election Center, an operation of the National Association of Election Officials. Trump toyed with meddling The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering federal elections. Congress may override state election regulations, but the president has no unilateral authority over how elections are run. Despite that, Trump made repeated attempts to assert such authority, including by signing executive orders attempting to impose a federal proof of citizenship requirement to vote and directing the U.S. Postal Service to impose restrictions on ballots sent through the mail. Major portions of both orders have been blocked by federal courts. The U.S. Supreme Court halted the mail-ballot restrictions for the midterms, but their legality for the 2028 election remains unsettled. Charles Stewart III, a professor of political science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said the federal government was often “feckless” in its efforts to bend the election system. The decentralized nature of the electoral system — where states run their elections — also helped protect it, he said, against a “federal government that lacked the capacity to do a lot of things folks were worried about.” The Trump administration launched an array of legal challenges in the leadup to the election. For months, the U.S. Department of Justice pursued dozens of lawsuits seeking sensitive voter data from states, though none have been successful. Weeks before Election Day, the DOJ sued California to force the state to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizen voters. It also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race, and demanded ballots be set aside in Washington state. Federal judges blocked the legal challenges in California and Alaska, and a judge prohibited the DOJ from forcing election officials to segregate ballots in Washington state. Guy-Uriel Charles, a professor of law at Harvard Law School, said that in many ways, the pre-election litigation was a good development. “Instead of going and putting troops or agents at the polls … the Trump administration litigated their disputes,” Charles said. Blue wave swept out challenges As the results were counted, the broad nature of the Democrats’ wins tamped down on the possibility of a chaotic post-election period, the panelists said. At least at the national level, very few high-profile contests were extremely close, leaving less room for legal fights or claims of fraud. The wide margins allowed news organizations to call enough races that it became clear within hours of the first polls closing that Democrats would take control of Congress. That meant that the few exceptionally close races, like the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi, didn’t determine which party controls the chamber — reducing scrutiny of the elections in those states. But if control of the Senate had hinged on Mississippi, the tight election in that state could have spiraled into a national controversy, some of the panelists indicated. Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by only a few dozen votes on election night. The Associated Press didn’t call the race for Colom until more than a week later, when he had a lead of 4,669 votes, or about 0.5 percentage points. The state has no recount law, meaning that any recount would only occur if ordered by a court. Election officials also used data from the credit agency Experian to list voters as inactive, which required them to sign affidavits when they voted. Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project and the moderator of the panel discussion, said that if Mississippi had decided control of the Senate and the national press had descended on the state and seen its election administration problems, “We would be in big trouble.” Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson, a Republican, has defended the affidavit system. In an opinion column posted to his official website on Monday, Watson wrote that approximately 75% of affidavits were approved and counted. Charles said the midterms reflected an electorate that wanted to send a “very clear message.” But he cautioned that the message may not always be so clear. “We can’t count on that next time around, and I think there’s some warnings here that we must heed,” Charles said, “notwithstanding the great work by a number of people trying to assure that this election went as smoothly as possible.”

articles.title: Ars Live: What do drone strikes on data centers mean for the future? Talk at 1 pm EST today
articles.description: Ars Live discussion is happening today, November 17, at 1 pm Eastern Time.
articles.content: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.Read full article Comments

Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.description: AI agent takes unapproved actions even when laptop lid is closed and told not to.
articles.content: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”Read full article Comments

Lansing City Council hears calls for emergency homelessness response, delays action
articles.description: In the wake of a sweep of a homeless encampment in Lansing’s Old Town neighborhood, city council members heard hours of public testimony calling for a broader response to homelessness as winter weather approaches.
articles.content:
Khadja Erickson, the executive director of the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center speaks about the need for greater support for the unhoused community in Lansing, including a proposed moratorium on encampment sweeps, at a council meeting on Nov. 16, 2026.
(Katherine Dailey / Michigan Advance)In the wake of a sweep of a homeless encampment in Lansing’s Old Town neighborhood, city council members heard hours of public testimony calling for a broader response to homelessness as winter weather approaches.Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez, who represents the city’s second ward, has proposed an ordinance to enact a 60-day moratorium on sweeps of homeless encampments in certain city parks. It would not apply to sweeps on private property, such as the most recent sweep, which took place on Thursday.Nevarez Martinez was clear that she does not believe such a moratorium is a permanent or long-term solution to homelessness, but that time is needed to develop a strategy and identify shelter options for those facing homelessness.“We do not have sufficient options for people, and then we criminalize them for having nowhere else to go. That is unacceptable. I believe we need to address this crisis on multiple fronts: sufficient low-barrier emergency shelter, transitional housing, and permanently affordable housing,” she said. “My goal is not to pit our unhoused neighbors against our housed residents, our schools, or our business community, we all have a stake in making Lansing a safer, healthier, and more compassionate city.”Meanwhile, Council President Peter Spadafore has introduced a resolution to establish an ad hoc committee on homelessness strategy. The resolution was expected to come before the council Monday, but Spadafore said email issues had delayed its consideration until the next meeting.Both the moratorium and the establishment of the committee are expected to be considered on Dec. 7, the next meeting of the council.Nick Cook, the director of public policy at the Michigan Coalition Against Homelessness, was among the many speaking during the public comment period who emphasized the harms that can be done to residents in an encampment when it is swept.“Let’s be honest about what is happening. People are not sleeping in tents because they want to; they are sleeping in tents because there’s nowhere else to go. Shelters are full. Affordable housing is scarce. Supportive housing is insufficient,” Cook said. “Yet, instead of addressing those realities, our response has too often been to push people from one piece of public property to another and call it progress. It is not progress. An encampment sweep does not house a single person. Does not treat mental illness. Does not help someone find employment. It does not connect people to stability. What it does is scatter vulnerable people, destroy what little property they have left, sever ties with outreach workers, and make survival even harder.”Many also focused on the long-term solutions necessary to address homelessness in a sustainable fashion — and the fact that the city council has had repeated hearings about the same issues in recent months.“If you want encampments to go away, the solution is very simple. It’s housing. That’s how you prevent them from returning,” Khadja Erickson, the executive director of the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center, said. “That’s how you prevent from experiencing this: a bunch of people coming to talk to you about homelessness. I promise you, I am just as tired of talking about it as you are of hearing about it.”Erickson, along with others, also repeatedly noted that a more long-term response was necessary, especially one that allows better access to wraparound services, as well as access to water and safe heating sources.“You keep lauding these 70 shelter beds. As many people have come up here and said, in 2026 we found over 800 people in our point-in-time count,” Erickson said. “70 beds is not even 10% of that number.”Multiple members of Lansing’s unhoused community also spoke at the meeting.One speaker, who identified himself as a disabled combat veteran, argued that people experiencing homelessness are already living throughout the city and should be allowed to remain where they are. He said existing shelters are inadequate and described the Capital City Rescue Mission’s requirements and crowded conditions and said he would rather remain outdoors than stay in those conditions.Alyssa Clark, who identified herself as a small business owner near the recently-swept encampment, said that she has had clients cancel appointments and “question whether they feel safe coming here.”“Over the past nine months, we’ve dealt with people sleeping in fire escapes, unattended fires, encampments in the parking lot, discarded needles, trash, human waste, and recurring sewage problems. These aren’t just inconveniences; they’re serious safety and sanitation concerns that are affecting my business,” she said.However, most speakers emphasized the humanity of those who are facing homelessness and the need for people to have a safe location to go if there are encampment sweeps.Reverend Elijah Burton, pastor of First Christian Church in Lansing, said that he was present at Thursday’s sweep and was angry about the treatment of unhoused individuals in Lansing.“What kind of refuge requires someone to pack up their life every morning? What kind of safety exists when people must constantly fear being displaced?” Burton asked. “We have become so concerned with the visibility of homelessness that we are losing sight of the actual crisis. People do not have homes. Moving someone does not house them. Removing a tent does not create a shelter bed somewhere, and making people disappear from our parks does not make homelessness disappear from our city.”Michigan Advance is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.
