Commentary: Lame duck ultimatum: Get kratom off Michigan’s store shelves
articles.description: There is always a great deal of lip service about protecting our children. But when it comes down to it in Lansing, political clout and profit seems to matter more. Children make up a small percentage of our state’s population, but they are 100 percent of our collective future. Eight months have passed since the […]
articles.content: Liquid kratom extracts and capsules containing 7-OH are displayed for sale at a smoke shop in Buffalo, N.Y. A growing market is prompting state lawmakers to reconsider how the substance should be regulated. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)There is always a great deal of lip service about protecting our children. But when it comes down to it in Lansing, political clout and profit seems to matter more. Children make up a small percentage of our state’s population, but they are 100 percent of our collective future. Eight months have passed since the Michigan House of Representatives voted to ban kratom. As the Legislature enters its final lame duck stretch of 2026, an addictive, unregulated substance remains as easy for a teenager to buy as a Snickers bar. Sold in brightly colored packaging — tonics, tablets, powders, gummies, even chocolate bars and honey sticks — at neighborhood gas stations, party stores and smoke shops, kratom and its concentrated cousins, colloquially known as “gas station heroin,” are hiding in plain sight. Not a harmless herb with a dangerous cousin — one product line, one pathway The kratom industry wants Michigan to believe there are two separate products: a gentle, centuries-old herbal leaf and a dangerous lab-made outlier. Ban the bad one, they say, and leave the leaf alone. That is a distinction designed to protect a business model, not our kids. Kratom-infused drinks are stacked in a refrigerator at a smoke shop in Howard County, Md. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline) Kratom comes from the Southeast Asian Mitragyna speciosa tree. Its leaf acts on the same brain receptors as opioids, and it is marketed as a pain reliever, an energy and mood booster, and a treatment for anxiety, depression and even withdrawal from heroin and fentanyl. It is habit-forming in its own right. Manufacturers have also flooded the market with chemically manipulated, concentrated variants such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) — a compound present only in trace amounts in the natural leaf but now sold in pills and shots far more potent than morphine. The pharmacological effects of these products, along with their withdrawal symptoms and overdose profiles, closely mirror those of prescription and illicit opioids. The leaf and the concentrate are not separate worlds. They sit on the same shelves, sold by the same stores, often under the same brand names. The leaf is the on-ramp; the concentrate is where too many people end up. And because there is no state testing or regulatory oversight for any of these products, consumers — especially children — have no way of knowing the potency or chemical makeup of what they are swallowing. The vulnerability of developing young brains and central nervous systems makes children and teenagers especially susceptible to acute toxicity, severe neurological side effects and rapid dependency. Today, we are playing Russian roulette with the safety of our children, families and communities. The data are stark: state lawmakers report that kratom was detected in 995 of nearly 2,000 overdose deaths in Michigan during 2024, alongside a reported 1,200 percent surge in national use driven by accessible, over-the-counter gummies and concentrates. As a former state superintendent of Michigan’s schools, former state mental health director, and former president and CEO of Detroit Wayne Integrated Health Network (DWIHN), the largest community mental health agency in Michigan, I have had a front-row seat watching children and families devastated by the scourge of addictive drugs. We are allowing companies to profit off the suffering of children and our fellow citizens. A Michigan mother’s warning This past Sunday night, 60 Minutes brought this crisis into living rooms across America, and the human face of the story was one of our own. Correspondent Jon Wertheim profiled Melanie Clark, a Michigan mother of three and trained opera singer. Struggling with postpartum depression and exhaustion, she was drawn in by Instagram ads for a kratom-based “tonic” sold at gas stations near her home. Notice where her story starts: not with a lab-made 7-OH tablet, but with a kratom drink marketed as a wellness product. Within about three weeks, she felt addicted. After trying to quit, she relapsed and moved on to 7-OH tablets, which landed her in the hospital. Her withdrawal was so severe that her husband had to call the police. Thankfully, she says she is doing much better today. Melanie’s story should stop every lawmaker in Lansing cold. If kratom can ensnare a grown woman with a supportive family, imagine what it can do to a 15-year-old with a few dollars in their pocket and a gas station on their walk home from school. Why House Bill 5537 gets it right In March 2026, the Michigan House passed House Bill 5537 by a vote of 56–48. The bill does what a partial approach cannot: it prohibits growing, synthesizing, distributing and selling kratom in every form — the plant, its leaves, its extracts, and its synthetic and concentrated derivatives — while exempting FDA-approved products. It carries misdemeanor penalties, with stiffer consequences for selling to minors. Banning only 7-OH would invite a game of chemical whack-a-mole: outlaw one derivative and manufacturers will reformulate the next one, while the leaf products that start people down this road stay on the counter next to the candy. Getty Images Plus The bill was quickly sent to the Senate Committee on Government Operations — known around the Capitol as a place for bills to die — and has sat there ever since. Lansing insiders say there has been heavy pushback from lobbyists for kratom manufacturers and from gas station and party store owners. Because 2026 marks the end of Michigan’s two-year legislative term, inaction in lame duck is not a harmless pause; it is a fatal reset. If the Senate adjourns without acting, HB 5537 dies, forcing lawmakers to start over in 2027 while another class of middle and high school students is exposed. Washington is moving backward Nor can Michigan wait for Washington. As 60 Minutes reported, the federal government announced plans in July to schedule 7-OH as a controlled substance. Then last month, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services reversed course and raised the amount of 7-OH allowed in products roughly twentyfold. Former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary and former HHS senior adviser Calley Means both told the program they resigned in part because kratom policy was being shaped by business interests rather than public health. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE HHS denies that outside pressure influenced its decision, but 60 Minutes also documented a decade of lobbying money, much of it from the American Kratom Association, aimed at the FDA, HHS, the White House and Congress. Note what that lobbying protects: the industry’s preferred line is to sacrifice 7-OH and save the leaf. When federal protection is moving backward, states must lead. A local patchwork is not enough Communities have stepped up where the state has not. To its credit, Sterling Heights in May became the first city in Michigan to ban the sale and distribution of all kratom products — not just the synthetics — threatening to revoke the licenses of businesses that don’t comply. Plymouth Township has followed with restrictions of its own. But a municipal ban does little good when a teenager can drive five minutes across a city line to the nearest gas station. Only statewide action can close that loophole and hold predatory distributors accountable. Michigan is also falling behind. A growing list of states, including Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Vermont and Wisconsin, ban kratom outright, and many more restrict sales to minors. Decades ago, Michigan watched the prescription opioid crisis spiral out of control because regulators hesitated while corporations profited from addiction. We cannot afford to repeat that tragedy. The ask The American Kratom Association and other opponents argue for age limits and labeling rules instead of prohibition. I understand that some adults say kratom helped them through pain or off other opioids, and their struggles are real. The answer for them is real treatment and FDA-approved medicine — which this bill exempts — not an unregulated product sold beside the Slurpee machine. Labels and age rules on a product no one tests will not keep it out of children’s hands. Protecting Michigan’s youth is not a Republican or Democratic issue; it is a basic moral obligation. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has goodwill to spend and should spend some of it saving children, families and communities. House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) and Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) must rise above partisan gridlock, move HB 5537 across the finish line, and take kratom in all its forms off store shelves before the 2026 session closes. Our children and families need more than political posturing or infighting. Without action, unnecessary misery, and even death, will be on the hands of our elected officials. Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption
articles.description: Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption AP News Mongolian president announces resignation over alleged corruption Reuters Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa to resign amid corruption allegations DW.com Mongolian President Abruptly Resigns After Alleged Misconduct Bloomberg.com Mongolia’s president to resign over railway corruption allegations Financial Times
articles.content: ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia (AP) — Mongolia’s President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he will resign after another politician from the ruling Mongolian People’s Party accused him of benefiting financially from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister. The announcement came after Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of Ulaanbaatar, the country’s capital, on Saturday accused Khurelsukh of receiving 25 million dollars in connection with the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project. The former mayor belongs to a different faction of the same party as the president. Following the accusations, the opposition Democratic Party then called for Khurelsukh to resign. Khurelsukh rejected accusations of wrongdoing and said in an address to the nation on Tuesday that he had faced sustained attacks on his reputation for more than a month, even as he said he would resign. “I have never stolen from my people or my state,” he said. “I will hand over my duties as president and become an ordinary citizen.” He said he would cooperate with investigators. Mongolia’s Deputy Minister of Justice and Home Affairs Munkh-Erdene Dembereltseren and the head of the Cabinet secretariat, Enkhbayar Battumur, who were also mentioned in the accusations, said on Tuesday they will also resign. The allegations say that Khurelsukh ensured the railway contract was awarded in 2019 to Bodi International LLC, one of the country’s biggest conglomerates, without a competitive tender and that he had received money in bribes from the company. On Monday, Bodi denied in a statement that it had paid any cash bribes to senior government officials and civil servants, saying the allegations were defamatory and that the company had not done anything wrong. One expert characterized the resignation as a power play, so that Khurelsukh could perhaps try to run for another office later on, noting that the resignation will play well with the public. “In the public face, he looks just and honest, and a good politician,” said Munkh-Erdene Gantulga, a lecturer at the National University of Mongolia. Khurelsukh resigned in January 2021 when he served as prime minister so that he could run for president, Gantulga said. He won six months later and his Mongolian People’s Party won a majority in the legislature at the same time. But the party has been beset by infighting in recent years, with Mongolia seeing three prime ministers taking office in just nine months. Khurelsukh’s resignation would take effect once it is accepted by parliament, known as the State Great Khural. The body is expected to meet later this week to vote on his resignation. If accepted, the speaker of the parliament will serve as interim president. Still, it appears that the political storm may not end quickly. The president’s accuser, Nyambaatar, who has been reported to be living abroad — likely in Canada — said on his Facebook page that he has been followed by suspicious-looking people. He warned Khurelsukh not to try to conduct a covert operation on foreign soil and also said he would “expose further unimaginable acts of theft and corruption that have been concealed under the guise of state secrets” in upcoming livestreams. Associated Press writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report. A previous version of this story was corrected to show that the accusation of corruption came from a member of a faction of the ruling party, not from an opposition party.

articles.title: What is WebRTC? A guide to real-time web communication
articles.description: Learn what WebRTC is, how it works, and how STUN, TURN, and media servers fit in. Compare WebRTC vs WebSocket and see use cases and limitations.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Seamless web communication feels effortless today. But building a low-latency video or voice streaming app used to be a major hurdle for developers. Users had to deal with dropped frames, audio lag, and disconnections that marred interactions. WebRTC helps developers address shortcomings in real-time web communications by enabling low-latency peer-to-peer data streaming. Since its introduction in 2011, major browsers, including Chrome, Safari, and Firefox, have adopted WebRTC. Today, WebRTC supports real-time communication in browsers and web apps. This article explores how WebRTC works, its use cases, security considerations, and how it compares with other web communication technologies. WebRTC is a free, open-source communication technology that enables peer-to-peer, real-time streaming between web browsers. With WebRTC, users can exchange video, audio, and data directly without downloading plugins or intermediary software. Unlike traditional client-server streaming, WebRTC sends media directly between peers whenever a direct path exists. Relay (TURN) servers and media servers step in only when a direct connection isn’t possible or when more than two participants join. This allows WebRTC to deliver low-latency real-time media. Modern web browsers support WebRTC by default. WebRTC is an open standard from the W3C and IETF that exposes JavaScript APIs, which let you access the camera and microphone, create a data channel, and deliver media content to the destination. Because of its simplicity, developers use WebRTC to power various web applications, including teleconferencing, video and audio streaming, real-time transcription, and screen sharing. WebRTC captures data in a browser, encrypts it, and streams it to another browser in real time. It creates a data channel over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), where browsers or web apps can exchange data with low latency. UDP is a fast, connectionless protocol that sends data packets across networks. It doesn’t need to maintain a connection, acknowledge packet reception, or retransmit lost packets, resulting in significantly lower overhead. By default, the native WebRTC API supports direct peer-to-peer (P2P) streaming between two browsers. However, more than two browsers can exchange data by creating multiple P2P connections or using a media server. Often, upstream bandwidth limits multiple P2P connections, making a media server a better option for applications like live conferencing. Below, we use an example that demonstrates video between two browsers to explain how it works. To create a WebRTC connection, both browsers follow these sequences. The WebRTC standards provide application programming interfaces (API) and guidelines for media capture, data security, and media exchange. However, it doesn’t define a signaling framework. Therefore, developers implement signaling through different mechanisms, such as WebSockets. A codec is an algorithm that compresses and decompresses media streams. All WebRTC-compliant browsers must support the following codecs. However, some browsers may support newer codecs, such as AV1 and VP9. WebRTC exposes three core APIs to developers in the browser runtime. Most WebRTC connections happen between devices located in different networks. They need their peer’s public IP address to exchange data. However, devices are often located behind a firewall, router, or within a protected network. These devices don’t always know their public IP address, which complicates connection efforts. Routers use Network Address Translation (NAT) to map private addresses to a public one. WebRTC then uses Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) to find a working path between peers. NAT is a service that allows devices in a local network to share a single public IP address. For example, your computer has a private IP address of 192.168.1.104. With NAT, your router maps it to a public IP address of 210.195.229.181 when it connects to the internet. When you send a data packet to the public IP address, the router identifies the corresponding private IP address and local port and delivers the data to it. ICE is a framework that allows peer devices to discover each other. Devices will first attempt to establish a connection using the public IP address they discover through a STUN server. If that fails, they revert to an intermediary relay server. Both STUN and TURN servers operate within the ICE framework to enable successful peer connection. A media server is an intermediary server that routes data between devices in the WebRTC architecture. While a WebRTC media server isn’t mandatory, it is useful when a device needs to stream to multiple peers at once. A WebRTC media server offloads the burden of processing, encryption, and routing to destination devices. WebSocket is a protocol that allows bidirectional data exchange between a client and server. It runs over the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which provides reliable, ordered delivery. Meanwhile, WebRTC provides peer-to-peer streaming capabilities using UDP, which has lower latency and is optimized for real-time transmission. WebRTC is better when you want to stream high-definition video and cannot afford lag or degradation. Meanwhile, WebSocket is suitable for maintaining a persistent connection where applications can reliably exchange messages with the backend server. WebRTC and WebSocket are not competing protocols. In fact, to establish a WebRTC connection, devices use WebSockets for signaling. WebSocket is built for event-driven messages, allowing devices to send and receive networking parameters, media metadata, and other alerts. WebRTC has become the standard for low-latency streaming across web apps and browsers. Over the years, developers have leveraged WebRTC to support these applications. WebRTC is a set of APIs built on top of several protocols. Developers use WebRTC APIs that are built into browsers or available as SDKs to build low-latency voice and video streaming applications. For example, they call APIs like getUserMedia, RTCPeerConnection, and RTCDataChannel to establish RTC connections and exchange data bidirectionally. You can also think of WebRTC as a suite of protocols working together to enable real-time streaming. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Provides initial encryption and authentication handshaking to secure WebRTC data. Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) Encrypts WebRTC payloads that are being streamed to peer devices. Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Allows devices to send data in an orderly manner Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Enables a device to discover its public IP address, which it then sends to peer devices. Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Offers a relay address through an intermediary server that peers use if they fail to establish a direct connection. While WebRTC provides the fundamentals for streaming audio, video, or other data types, it is not a platform. WebRTC doesn’t provide the frameworks, infrastructure, or signaling mechanisms needed to facilitate data exchange. While WebRTC offers low-latency bidirectional communication, developers face several real-world implementation challenges. WebRTC faces a performance bottleneck when multiple participants join the mesh network. For example, if five participants join a live video conference, a device must stream video data to the other four participants at once. This stresses the computer's resources and bandwidth, eventually degrading streaming quality. Devices might not be able to establish a peer-to-peer connection using STUN if they’re behind firewalls or symmetric NAT. Symmetric NAT maps public-facing ports to specific destinations, which restricts peer-to-peer communication. In those cases, WebRTC falls back to TURN, which increases end-to-end latency. While WebRTC automatically encrypts data in transit, several challenges remain. Without a standardized signaling framework, developers may use different signaling mechanisms, which can lead to conflicting or misaligned negotiation messages. This can cause devices to try several times before successfully negotiating a WebRTC connection. ElevenAgents lets you build real-time voice agents that connect over WebRTC. In the JavaScript and React SDKs, voice conversations use WebRTC by default and text-only conversations use WebSocket. You can set connectionType to 'webrtc' or 'websocket' in startSession to choose explicitly. WebRTC is available in the React, Swift, and React Native SDKs, and in the Unity SDK on WebGL builds. WebRTC brings browser-native echo cancellation and background noise suppression, which helps keep audio clear in AI conversations. Learn more about ElevenAgents or contact sales to get started with conversational AI agents at scale. WebRTC is a peer-to-peer real-time streaming web technology for exchanging audio, video, and other arbitrary data. Meanwhile, WebSocket is an event-messaging protocol that allows bi-directional communication between server and client. WebRTC uses UDP to send data packets, while WebSocket relies on TCP. WebRTC exposes a device's private or public IP address to its peers. Without mitigation, this can raise security concerns. Additionally, devices might fail to establish a peer-to-peer connection, requiring a TURN server to act as an intermediary in a potentially complex and costly setup. Modern browsers, including Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari, and Microsoft Edge support WebRTC. They support core APIs like getUserMedia, RTCDataChannel, and RTCPeerConnection. While browsers support VP8 and H.264, support for newer codecs like VP9 and AV1 may vary. WebRTC provides a low-latency data transport layer that AI agents use to stream conversations with users. By running over UDP, a lost packet does not stall the stream, and a built-in jitter buffer streamlines the playback experience. Zoom uses WebRTC for parts of its browser-based client, alongside proprietary libraries. For one-to-one calls, Zoom may switch to WebRTC. However, Zoom’s desktop and mobile clients rely on proprietary technology instead of WebRTC. Zoom added WebRTC support to its Video SDK for web with version 2, announced in December 2024. This lets developers add WebRTC video conferencing to their apps using Zoom’s architecture. articles.title: Scribe v3 Live Medical helps conversational agents get clinical details right
articles.description: Scribe v3 Live Medical helps agents catch drug names and clinical terms on live calls, with the lowest WER of the medical models we tested.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. A voice agent acts on what it hears during a live call. When a patient says they take sitagliptin for diabetes, the agent can add it to their medication list for the clinician to review. But drug names are easy to mishear. In our testing, we saw a speech model transcribe sitagliptin as citalopram, an antidepressant. For many people, these calls are the first step in reaching their care team, and an agent can only help if it hears them correctly. Today, ElevenLabs is releasing Scribe v3 Live Medical, which brings medical transcription to live calls. It’s built on Scribe v3 Live, our newest real-time Speech to Text model, and optimized for clinical language. It’s available now in ElevenAgents. ElevenLabs already offers medical transcription for recorded audio, like dictation and visit recordings. But much of what healthcare teams build runs in real time, from scheduling and medical information lines to eligibility checks over the phone and claims follow-ups. Those calls can’t wait for a recording to end. Medication names and doses rarely come up in everyday speech, so they’re the words a general real-time model is more likely to get wrong. Scribe v3 Live Medical is our first medical transcription built for agents, carrying the clinical focus of Scribe v2 Medical into real-time conversations. In our tests on PriMock57, a public set of mock live doctor visits, Scribe v3 Live Medical made fewer errors than any other medical model we evaluated. Scribe v3 Live Medical is designed for patient, member, and provider calls where the details are clinical, like a medication at intake, a procedure on a prior authorization, or a symptom on a follow-up call. Many healthcare agents also handle calls with no clinical details at all, like rescheduling an appointment or asking about office hours. Scribe v3 Live Medical improves accuracy on clinical details and holds its accuracy on everyday speech, so teams can use it for every call. Healthcare teams can add up to 10,000 of their own terms, and Scribe v3 Live Medical draws on the list only when a caller seems to say one of them. That’s enough for a regional health system to load every provider and clinic name across its locations, or for a pharmaceutical company to load its full portfolio by brand and generic name. With a custom term list loaded, Scribe v3 Live Medical made up to 48% fewer errors on medical terms in our tests. Callers often read a member ID or date of birth in pieces, pausing between groups of digits as they find them on a card. An agent that treats every pause as the end of a turn jumps in mid-number, and the caller has to start again. Scribe v3 Live Medical recognizes when a number isn’t finished yet, so the agent waits for the rest before it replies. Patients and caregivers may switch languages mid-call, for example to describe a symptom more easily in their first language. Scribe v3 Live Medical supports more than 90 languages and follows those switches, so speech in a second language is transcribed instead of dropped. Teams are already building agents with Scribe v3 Live Medical. “The interaction experience with Eleven v4 Turbo and Scribe v3 Live Medical is phenomenal” says Idin Jafari, Director, Digital Strategy & Innovation at Pfizer. “The agent sounds realistic, and it’s more accurate on the brand and generic names that come up in our conversations.” On patient calls, that accuracy carries through to what care teams review after the call. “ElevenLabs keeps raising the bar, and that lets Vintage Labs move faster. Our VIA platform makes pre- and post-procedure calls for large academic health systems. With Scribe v3 Live Medical, it understands patients better: their medications, their procedures, the names of their doctors,” says Shantanu Ghorai, Founder & COO of Vintage Labs AI. “Turn detection waits for patients to finish their date of birth before replying, and multilingual mode keeps up when callers switch to Spanish. Nurses can now trust the call summary without replaying the recording.” We tested Scribe v3 Live Medical against real-time Speech to Text models from leading providers, including specialized medical models and general-purpose models, all on the same recordings. We used two public benchmarks of doctor-patient conversations, compared Scribe v3 Live Medical with Scribe v3 Live on medical and everyday speech, and tested medical terms in English, French, and German. Results are in English unless noted. We report word error rate (WER), the share of words transcribed incorrectly, and semantic WER, which counts only errors that change the meaning. Semantic WER treats “20 mg” and “twenty milligrams” as a match, so its scores run lower than WER. Note: These results come from ElevenLabs’ internal testing of selected providers in real-time mode, with each model in its best available configuration. They don’t include every available model. PriMock57 includes 57 mock live primary care consultations, about 9 minutes each, between clinicians and actors playing patients. The conversations were unscripted on both sides. Actors worked from case cards covering symptoms, medical history, and current medications, and clinicians ran each consultation as they would a real one. The calls ran over telemedicine software, with clinicians on laptops and patients on mobile phones, in an office environment with background noise. We used this benchmark because it has what makes patient calls hard to transcribe: unscripted back-and-forth conversations, phone audio with background noise, and dense clinical detail. Scribe v3 Live Medical had the lowest WER of the medical models we tested (12.8%), with 17% fewer errors than the next closest one. Fareez OSCE is 272 recorded patient interviews in the format medical schools use to test clinical skills, the Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE). In each one, a resident doctor or senior medical student asks someone playing the patient about their symptoms and history. Because a different team recorded it in another country, the set shows whether the results hold with new speakers, recording setups, and conditions. Scribe v3 Live Medical had the lowest semantic WER of the medical models we tested (0.6%). Eka Medical ASR contains more than 3,600 English recordings from doctors and medical students, focused on medical terms and branded drug names. Scribe v3 Live Medical made 4.7% fewer errors on Eka Medical ASR than Scribe v3 Live (11% vs. 11.54% semantic WER). Common Voice is Mozilla’s set of sentences read aloud by volunteers, and FLEURS is Google’s set of short, non-clinical sentences read in more than 100 languages. We scored both on their English sets to make sure teams using Scribe v3 Live Medical don’t give up accuracy on everyday speech. Even a sentence that names a drug is made up mostly of everyday words, so a medical model has to get both right. Scribe v3 Live Medical performs about the same as Scribe v3 Live on both. Many healthcare teams serve patients in more than one language. MED-Term, a public benchmark from Corti, is a set of spoken clinical case descriptions in English, French and German, each built around rare and specialized medical terms. We used it to check how Scribe v3 Live Medical handles clinical vocabulary beyond English. Its semantic WER was 2.24% in English, 2.81% in German, and 3.24% in French. On a live call, an agent can’t respond until it has the transcript, so any lag in transcription becomes a pause callers hear. Scribe v3 Live transcribes speech in about 150 milliseconds, and in testing, Scribe v3 Live Medical matches that latency, so its clinical focus adds no noticeable delay. Error rates are easier to judge on a real call. A 10-minute intake call runs about 1,500 words between the caller and the agent. At the PriMock57 error rates above, Scribe v3 Live Medical would get about 40 more of those words right than the next best medical model we tested. For a team handling 1,000 calls a day, that’s about 40,000 more words transcribed correctly every day. Not every word carries the same weight. A dropped “um” is harmless. A misheard medication puts the wrong drug on a refill request, and a wrong digit in a member ID stalls an eligibility check. Either one can turn into a callback, a transfer to staff, or a patient asked to repeat themselves. Healthcare agents hear protected health information (PHI) on many calls, including names, dates of birth, member IDs, medications, and symptoms. Scribe v3 Live Medical is HIPAA-eligible for enterprise customers with a business associate agreement (BAA) in place and Zero Retention Mode enabled. Scribe v3 Live Medical runs on ElevenAgents, which is covered by our compliance programs, including SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS Level 1. Patient data is stored in the US by default. Enterprise teams that need it stored outside the US can use isolated environments in the EU, India, or Singapore. Scribe v3 Live Medical is available today in ElevenAgents. Go to Settings > Automatic Speech Recognition and select it from the model dropdown. John is on the ElevenAgents growth team, with a focus on the healthcare industry. articles.content: Attendees of a Transgender Day of Visibility rally at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., on March 30, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance) This story was originally reported by Orion Rummler of The 19th. Meet Orion and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. A new study finds high satisfaction among transgender people who were prescribed hormone therapy in their youth, providing an important window into healthcare that has become increasingly politicized and banned across the country. The study, published in JAMA Pediatrics, surveyed 376 trans people who had all previously received gender-affirming care at the same unidentified clinic, which provided access to different specialists under one roof. Nearly 97 percent said that going on hormone therapy was the right decision, and 3 percent said they regretted their decision. Two percent said they were both harmed by going on hormones and regretted it. These findings are significant because politicians have tied efforts to ban gender-affirming care to stories of regret and harm among people who transition and then stop or reverse aspects of it. Republicans and the Trump administration have held up the existence of these people, known as detransitioners, as support for their efforts to ban gender-affirming care for minors. But studies have consistently found low regret rates for gender-affirming care for trans youth and adults, as well as benefits including improved emotional well-being years after receiving treatment. A 2024 study from Princeton, which analyzed the experiences of 220 transgender youth, found the majority were satisfied with and continuing gender-affirming care. Most participants in that study had been on puberty blockers for about five years and on hormones for nearly four years. Patients in this new study ranged from 14 to 28 years old, and most of them were still taking hormones at the time of the survey, which was taken on average five years after they had started hormone replacement therapy (HRT). Among the 65 people no longer on hormones, the majority still believed going on HRT was the right decision for them. Most participants started hormones when they were 17 or younger. The study was administered from 2023 to 2025 by researchers at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center as well as the Boston Children’s Hospital, the Lurie Children’s Hospital in Chicago and other universities. In recent years, several of these institutions have halted providing gender-affirming care for youth or faced political pressure to do so. This study is one of the largest yet to analyze satisfaction and regret among transgender people who transitioned in their youth. It does have some limitations: Researchers assessed satisfaction with starting hormone therapy, but not specific effects, and did not gauge why some people stopped taking hormones. Nearly 300 patients who initially consented to participate in the research also never finished the final survey. This doesn’t mean that everyone with an unknown experience regrets treatment — it may also be chalked up to institutional distrust or fear that the data would be weaponized. But it marks a significant loss of data, said Kinnon R. MacKinnon, a social scientist and associate professor in the School of Social Work at York University in Canada. He was not involved in the creation of this study. “When they discontinue treatment, or even if they have regret, they may feel shame and avoid further engagement with the clinic,” he said. The findings of the study align with existing research, MacKinnon said: Satisfaction for gender-affirming care is high, while regret and harm is low. Other findings also match prior studies, he said, like that nonbinary patients had more regret about starting hormones than binary trans people. Nine respondents in the survey described details of feeling regret or harm. Those experiences fell into three main categories: They no longer wanted the physical changes caused by hormone therapy, they had negative side effects, or they felt they had been inadequately prepared to make an informed decision about starting hormone therapy. These few qualitative responses highlight the need for clinicians to reinforce that treatment can be paused or discontinued at any time, while encouraging trans youth and their families to communicate their concerns, the authors of the study write. Overall, the authors write, the study supports existing standards of care for transgender youth, as laid out by the Endocrine Society and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health — two medical organizations that have come under fire by the Trump administration.

articles.title: States split over EPA’s proposal to drop greenhouse gas rules for power plants
articles.description: States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency released a proposal that contends it doesn’t have the authority to regulate power plant greenhouse gas emissions to address global climate change concerns. This would […]
articles.content: A coal-fired power plant operates in Centralia, Washington. States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas power plant standards. (Photo by the Washington Department of Ecology via Washington State Standard)States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency released a proposal that contends it doesn’t have the authority to regulate power plant greenhouse gas emissions to address global climate change concerns. This would rescind the agency’s own findings in 2015 that it had the authority to do so under a section of the Clean Air Act. If finalized and upheld by courts, the move would repeal remaining power plant greenhouse-gas emissions regulations for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units. The agency said it aims to maintain affordability and reliability of energy supplies. It follows a final EPA rule that went into effect Monday that partially repeals 2024 emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as well as requirements that states develop related plans. The proposed rule would go even further. A comment period for that measure closed earlier this month, generating over 165,000 comments, including from states, health and environmental groups, and private citizens. States, public health and environmental groups have also filed legal challenges to the EPA’s rollbacks. Some states said the EPA’s regulatory authority over fossil fuel emissions is overreach and would harm their economies, while others said such federal regulations are needed as states, tribes and local governments grapple with the health and costs of air pollution and climate change. In a joint comment submitted last week, the attorneys general of 22 mostly Democratic-leaning states plus Washington, D.C., and officials from New York City, Denver, Chicago and California’s Bay Area wrote that climate change is costly to state and local governments and imposes public health dangers. In the over-160-page letter, the states pointed to a consensus study report from the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine last year that concluded that human activity-initiated greenhouse gas emissions will lead to more climate change, “with the severity of expected change increasing with every ton of greenhouse gases emitted.” The attorneys general wrote that EPA is pushing its proposal despite such “unequivocal evidence, and the increasingly devastating climate harms” that state and local governments experience. They added that the proposal “has no basis in fact or law, would result in large-scale emission increases that will harm the States and Local Governments, and is an unlawful abdication of EPA’s responsibility under the Clean Air Act to protect public health and welfare.” But the attorneys general of West Virginia and 24 other largely Republican-leaning states contended that the proposal “properly reverses course on past EPA attempts to reshape the Nation’s electricity-generating sector.” It would “allow States to secure affordable, reliable, and environmentally responsible energy for their residents,” they added. North Dakota, which signed on to that letter, also submitted its own comment saying it strongly supports the supplemental proposal. The state noted that it has a specific interest in the issue, since it collects a coal conversion tax when power is generated from coal within the state, which then helps pay for school districts and other government services. The National Tribal Air Association, an organization of 162 tribes focused on air quality management policies and programs for American Indian and Alaska Native tribes, groups that have been disproportionately affected by emissions, submitted a comment opposing EPA’s actions. “Many fossil fuel-fired electric generating units are located on or near American Indian and Alaska Native communities, and Tribes and Tribal members may disproportionately bear the public health and environmental consequences of the increased greenhouse gas and other emissions that this proposal would permit,” the association wrote. Carrie Jenks, executive director of the Environmental & Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, noted that some ongoing court cases may affect the EPA rules. Jenks also said that states that support EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gases are typically the ones that also support their own authority to regulate them within their own programs. “Then there are groups of states that want EPA’s authority to be limited, if not eliminated,” adding that others argue that states can’t regulate their own sources of greenhouse gases. Over 70 medical and public health organizations also submitted comments in opposition to the rollbacks. The groups included the American Medical Association, the American Lung Association, and several state American Academy of Pediatrics chapters, who argued the changes would harm the health of children and other vulnerable groups. “Children, older adults, people who work outside, individuals with preexisting health conditions or who are pregnant, low-wealth communities and communities of color often experience disproportionate health harms stemming from climate change and extreme weather events,” the groups wrote. Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org. FDA approves pimicotinib for symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor
articles.content: On November 10, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration approved pimicotinib (Pimjetmi, EMD Serono, Inc.), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) for which surgical resection may cause worsening functional limitation or severe morbidity. Full prescribing information for Pimjetmi will be posted on Drugs@FDA. Efficacy was evaluated in MANEUVER (NCT05804045), a double-blind, randomized (2:1), placebo-controlled, international trial in patients with TGCT for whom surgical resection may cause dysfunction or serious complications. Eligible patients had a confirmed diagnosis of symptomatic TGCT with measurable disease with at least one lesion having a minimum size of 2 cm. Patients were randomized to pimicotinib 50 mg or placebo once daily. Randomization was stratified by geographic region (China versus non-China). The major efficacy outcome measure was overall response rate (ORR), as assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR) per RECIST v1.1 at Week 25. ORR was 56% (95% CI: 42, 68) in the pimicotinib arm and 3.2% (95% CI: 0.1, 17) in the placebo arm. Median duration of response (DOR) was not reached in the pimicotinib arm; 32 responders (91%) had a DOR ≥6 months and 27 (77%) had a DOR ≥12 months. In addition, statistically significant improvements were observed in the pimicotinib arm compared to the placebo arm at Week 25 across prespecified patient-reported and functional endpoints. Patients treated with pimicotinib experienced gains in active range of motion of the affected joint as measured by goniometry assessments, a reduction in worst pain as measured by the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) Worst Pain Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), and improved physical functioning as measured by the Patient-reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Physical Function T-score. The most common (>20%) adverse reactions were pruritus, rash, face edema, periorbital edema, fatigue, nausea, headache, and peripheral edema. The most common (>30%) lab abnormalities were creatine phosphokinase increased, lactate dehydrogenase increased, aspartate aminotransferase increased, lipase increased, cholesterol increased, amylase increased, and alanine aminotransferase increased. The prescribing information includes warnings and precautions for hepatotoxicity, embryo-fetal toxicity, and increased serum creatinine without affecting renal function. The recommended pimicotinib dosage is 50 mg orally once daily with or without food. This review was conducted under Project Orbis, an initiative of the FDA Oncology Center of Excellence. Project Orbis provides a framework for concurrent submission and review of oncology drugs among international partners. For this review, FDA collaborated with the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), Health Canada (HC), Israel's Ministry of Health (ImoH), Singapore's Health Sciences Agency (HSA), Switzerland's Swissmedic (SMC), and United Kingdom's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). The European Medicines Agency (EMA) was an official observer of this review. The applications may be undergoing the submission process or still be under review at the other regulatory agencies. This review used the Assessment Aid, a voluntary submission from the applicant to facilitate the FDA’s assessment. Pimicotinib received fast track and breakthrough therapy designation. A description of FDA expedited programs is in the Guidance for Industry: Expedited Programs for Serious Conditions-Drugs and Biologics. Healthcare professionals should report all serious adverse events suspected to be associated with the use of any medicine and device to FDA’s MedWatch Reporting System or by calling 1-800-FDA-1088. For assistance with single-patient INDs for investigational oncology products, healthcare professionals may contact OCE’s Project Facilitate at 240-402-0004 or email OncProjectFacilitate@fda.hhs.gov.

articles.title: MSU working with FBI to investigate Nov. 3 cybersecurity threat
articles.content: A Michigan State University Testing Center room inside of Bessey Hall in East Lansing, Mich., on April 23, 2026. Michigan State University is investigating the Nov. 3 cybersecurity threat with local, state and federal authorities, including the FBI, according to a campuswide email from MSU IT. As of now, an assessment of the potential threat reveals that contact and demographic information for some current and former students, along with employees, were possibly exposed. However, MSU IT said that there is no current threat to campus that requires further action. The email also referenced resources on how to stay internet-safe, including a webpage that provides current updates on the situation and information about how students and staff can be extra vigilant and protect their data. More information about the strategies to protect data and devices can be found here. A separate cybersecurity incident on Oct. 1 prompted MSU to send an email urging faculty, staff and students to reset their NetID passwords. The ransomware gang BYOD claims to be responsible for the cybersecurity incident after adding MSU to its site on Nov. 2, saying it stole data from 1.3 million current and former MSU students. BYOD also claims to be behind the cyberattack that shut down a University of New Mexico hospital in October. "And at this time, we have no reason to believe the situation from Oct. 1 is linked with the current investigation," MSU Spokesperson Emily Guerrant told The State News.
